item.title: Burn the fleet, keep the semicolon
item.description: A civilisation rarely declines because it forgets how to build ships. It declines because it decides that building ships is not the sort of thing serious people do.
item.content:encoded:
In 1405 a Chinese fleet left Nanjing that no other power on earth could have assembled. Zheng He’s ships made seven voyages over 28 years, reaching Hormuz and the Swahili coast half a century before a Portuguese caravel managed the same water going the other way. Then it stopped. Within a few years of the Xuande emperor’s death in 1435 the civil bureaucracy had dissolved the naval offices, broken up the seagoing vessels and closed the routes.

The comfortable version blames hidebound Confucian xenophobes. The better version, argued by Yiu Siu in the Journal of Chinese History, will be wearily familiar to anyone who has sat on a budget committee. The emperor had built the fleet as an off-books enterprise: the tax system paid for it, the palace kept the trade profits. The mandarinate was funding a business it could never book revenue from. So when a child emperor came to the throne and their moment arrived, the bureaucrats did not merely stop the voyages. They built a fiscal firewall to stop any future emperor trying it again.

The most capable maritime organisation on earth was dismantled by intelligent people optimising correctly inside a badly drawn set of incentives. Nobody in the room was stupid. That is the whole problem.

15th Century Gateway Review

Any system that rewards conformity to inherited form over judgement about substance will eventually be overtaken by one that does not — because only the second kind can notice when the map has stopped matching the territory. The first kind has hired, promoted and ennobled people specifically for their fluency with the map. Asking them to look up is asking them to write down their own assets.

You see the junior version of this every week. The Bluebook is a citation system with a priesthood, a schism and a new edition every few years for reasons no practising lawyer has satisfactorily explained. Methodology has become a status word — a section you write to prove you are the sort of person who writes one. None of it began as vanity: citation formats exist so a reader can find the source, house style so a document can be read quickly by someone who did not draft it. The failure is the substitution. At some point the apparatus stopped asking does this work and started asking is this correct, and only the second question comes with a marking rubric.

So the semicolon gets policed and the clause that quietly reallocates the risk does not. Nobody in recorded history has been harmed by a comma splice. People are ruined every day by contracts drafted immaculately in the wrong direction.

Why heirs are a macroeconomic problem

Intelligence is substantially heritable. It is not transmissible. Galton worked out the difference in 1886 and gave us the phrase: regression to the mean. Clever parents have clever children, but on average less so. It is arithmetic, not ideology, and it is the single most reliably ignored fact in the history of elites.

Now add the behaviour of every parent who ever loved a child. Advantage passes down whole while ability regresses, and the gap between the position inherited and the ability inherited has to be filled with something. What fills it is form: the right school, the right register, the right way of holding a fork at the right sort of lunch. Credentialism is not a symptom of a stratified society. It is the load-bearing structure — the mechanism by which a mediocre heir is made legible as a superior person.

The cost is not moral, it is measured in output. Hsieh, Hurst, Jones and Klenow estimated in Econometrica that between a fifth and two-fifths of the growth in American output per person from 1960 to 2010 came from nothing more exotic than letting women and black men into the professions. Not from inventing anything. From no longer excluding people who were already there. Running the same logic forward, Bell, Chetty and colleagues found children of top-1% families are about ten times likelier to become inventors than children from below-median families — and the gap persists between children with the same early-childhood maths scores. The talent was measured. It was present. It simply was not in the room where inventing happens.

A society that hands positions to heirs is not being unfair in some abstract way that need trouble nobody. It is choosing to run at three-fifths capacity, and then wondering aloud why the other lot are building the ships.

A worked example

Which brings us, with a certain grim inevitability, to Donald Trump — interesting not as a villain but as a specimen. Villains are rare and usually competent. He is the purest available demonstration of what happens when a society’s machinery for identifying merit has been replaced by machinery for laundering inheritance.

A New York Times investigation in 2018, built on over a hundred thousand pages of records, found he received the equivalent of at least $413m from his father. His companies then filed for bankruptcy six times. Enterprise involves failure and there is no shame in a collapsed venture, but there is something very special about going bankrupt while running a casino. The house is meant to win. That is not a strategy, it is the architecture of the building.

He has said for decades that he graduated first in his class at Wharton. The dean’s list for his cohort is public. It is 56 names long. He is not on it, nor among the honours recipients in the 1968 commencement programme. He is simply an insecure liar who did not attend the top of his class and has spent sixty years citing it. In 2016 he paid $25m to settle fraud claims over Trump University. In 2024 a New York court found he had inflated asset values for years; an appellate panel threw out the penalty as unconstitutionally excessive in August 2025, but the fraud finding stood. And on 2 January 2021, recorded, he asked Georgia’s secretary of state for a number: “I just want to find 11,780 votes.”

Not count. Find.

A man who believes he actually won asks for a recount. Requesting a specific quantity is the behaviour of someone who has spent a lifetime discovering that the form can be made to say whatever is required, because nobody in his world was ever checking the substance. It worked on lenders. It worked on licensees. It worked on television. It worked on voters. Why would it not work on a state?

Why this style of leadership always loses in the end

In a few years it will be remarkably difficult to find anyone who admits to having supported Trump and his cronies.

This is not a prediction, it is a pattern with a very good record. In 1945 France discovered it had been, almost to a man, a nation of resisters — a retrospective unanimity so complete that Henry Rousso eventually had to coin a word for it, résistancialisme. The Communist Party styled itself the party of the 75,000 martyrs; the real figure was likely a few thousand. In occupied Germany, former party members obtained testimonials of clean political conduct from neighbours and victims, and the Germans, who are good at naming things, called them Persilscheine — Persil certificates, after the laundry detergent. Washed clean. Eight and a half million people had joined the Nazi Party. By 1949 you could not find them.

And this is where the argument closes on itself, because the disappearance is not merely hypocrisy. It is a measurement failure of exactly the kind that burned the fleet.

A leader who demands loyalty can only ever grade its form: the salute, the applause, the sufficiently enthusiastic public statement. He cannot measure the substance, because the one honest signal — someone willing to tell him he is wrong — is the first thing his system selects out. So he counts salutes and books them as a constituency. The numbers look magnificent right up to the morning they turn out to have been denominated in a currency nobody was actually holding. Ask Mr. Putin about his Ukrainian intelligence briefings.

Nor is the man at the top placed to notice. The figurehead is rarely the author of these arrangements; he is what they select for — the sociopath with enough nerve to take the job and not enough sense to see where it ends. He believes the salutes because nothing in his life has ever obliged him to check one, and checking is precisely the faculty the apparatus was built to filter out.

That is why these regimes do not decline gracefully. They are load-bearing right until they are vapour. The apparatus that grades form cannot see its own collapse coming, because collapse is a fact about substance and it stopped collecting that data years ago.

The Ming had the ships. Britain, before Crimea shamed it into competitive examination, had the officers. America has the best-trained professional workforce ever assembled. In none of these cases was the defect capability. The defect was governance — the slow, reasonable, minuted decision to reward fidelity to a form over judgement about a substance, until nobody in the building was being paid to notice that the map had come loose from the territory.

The fleets do not burn because somebody hates ships. They burn because the meeting ran to schedule, the paperwork was in order, and the item was carried.

item.title: Jackpot
item.description: AKA How to hack a democracy.
item.content:encoded:
You have been told that this is an orientation. It is not. Orientation is for people who have arrived somewhere by accident. You were selected, and you were selected a long time before you noticed us noticing you. So sit, and let me tell you what you have joined, starting at the beginning, because the beginning is the part everyone gets wrong.

We did not seize anything. That is the first correction. There was no coup, no smoke-filled room, no single afternoon on which the world changed hands. There was a curriculum.

Consider the position of a manufacturer in 1935. The Wagner Act had just made it the law of the land that his own workers could organise against him, and the men who wrote that law were popular. Not tolerated — popular. He could buy a senator; he could not buy the mood of a country that had watched capitalism fall over and had drawn the obvious conclusion. Our predecessors at the National Association of Manufacturers understood, earlier than anyone, that the mood was the asset. Everything else was downstream.

So they got in front of it. In 1935, the year of the Act itself, they put a radio serial on the air called The American Family Robinson, in which a sensible small-town newspaper editor patiently corrected the errors of cranks and planners, week after week, for years, given free to any station that would take it — three hundred of them did — with the air time paid by local sponsors who thought they were buying entertainment. It was not very good. It did not need to be. It was the largest single item in the Association’s budget and it was never once described as advertising. Two years later came the billboards: There’s no way like the American Way, a well-dressed family in a motor car above a caption about the world’s highest standard of living, on hoardings in hundreds of towns where the standard of living was nothing of the sort. Then the war did us the enormous favour of rehabilitating industry, and when the war ended, our predecessors did not go back to selling steel. They went back to selling the frame.

The fifteen years after 1945 were the most productive in our history and almost nobody has heard of them. Plant newspapers. Films shown in company time. Economics courses for foremen — How Our Business System Operates — and the same material, softened, for schoolteachers at summer conferences paid for by firms whose names were never on the letterhead. Sermon material for clergy. Advertising Council spots on free enterprise running alongside the war-bond drives. The historians who eventually noticed called it selling free enterprise, which is accurate but flatters us. We were not selling a product. We were installing a grammar — a set of sentences about markets and freedom and government that would feel, to a person who had absorbed them at seventeen, not like an argument but like the weather.

And while that was happening in the plants, something more durable was happening in the seminar rooms. In 1946 a chamber-of-commerce man named Leonard Read set up the Foundation for Economic Education, funded by businessmen who understood that they were buying something they would never live to see delivered. The year before, Reader’s Digest had condensed a difficult Austrian book about the road to serfdom into twenty pages and posted it to millions of American homes; the author was a marginal figure who had expected to be ignored. In 1947 he brought thirty-eight like-minded men (and one woman) to a hotel above Lake Geneva and founded a society that met, argued and published for decades while achieving nothing whatsoever. American money paid the airfares. By 1950 the same money had bought him a chair at Chicago, and went on paying his salary there for ten years. By 1974 he had a Nobel prize, and by 1980 his students were writing budgets.

Thirty years. I want you to sit with that number, because it is the number that separates us from every other faction that has ever wanted to run the world. Thirty years of funding a losing argument, patiently, through the entire period in which the losing argument was a joke.

Then the mood turned, and we were the only people in the building with a plan.

In August 1971 a corporate lawyer named Lewis Powell wrote a confidential memorandum for the Chamber of Commerce arguing that the American business system was under broad attack and that business had responded with appeasement. He proposed something quite specific: not lobbying, which is retail, but the long capture of the institutions that manufacture legitimacy — universities, the courts, television, the scholarly journals. Two months later he was nominated to the Supreme Court. Within eighteen months the Business Roundtable existed, so that chief executives could lobby in person rather than through hirelings. In 1973 a brewer’s money founded the Heritage Foundation, which differed from every think-tank before it in one respect: it did not exist to produce research. It existed to produce legislation, pre-drafted, arriving on a desk within twenty-four hours of the need for it. In 1977 a fortune made in oil and pipelines founded Cato. In 1981 an Englishman who had built a small institute in London on Hayek’s personal advice — do not go into politics, go into ideas — established Atlas, and did the single most intelligent thing anyone in our history has done. He franchised it. Not one think-tank; a method for producing think-tanks, exported to every capital that had a currency worth taking. There are hundreds now. Most of the people who work in them have no idea they are downstream of a man who started out selling battery chickens — and who was shown how to farm them, as it happens, by an introduction made through the Foundation for Economic Education. The money that built the London institute, and then the hundreds, came out of the first think-tank by way of a shed full of hens. I have always found that the most instructive sentence in our history.

In 1980 Heritage handed the incoming administration a thousand-page book called Mandate for Leadership. Within a year they were claiming that most of it had been adopted. They were exaggerating. Not by much.

That was the first phase, and it ended, as all our phases end, because reality intruded.

The reality was 1988. A NASA scientist told a Senate committee, in a hot June, that he was 99% certain the heat that summer was not natural variation — and then, having said the careful thing, went on and named the cause. The IPCC was constituted the same year. And for the first time since the war we faced a problem that could not be handled with a better grammar, because it was not an opinion. It was a measurement.

So we did what we do. In 1989 the Global Climate Coalition was assembled, and it was run out of our own offices — the Association’s offices, the same building, the same telephones. The histories cannot agree on when it moved out. They say 1992. Others say it was still there in 1997. I was there, and I can tell you that the question is meaningless, because the address on the letterhead was never the point. When the Rio summit produced a framework convention in 1992, that was written up internally as a defeat, because it was a defeat. But that it was also the making of us, because it forced us to abandon persuasion for something far cheaper.

In 1995 our own scientific advisory committee prepared a seventeen-page primer for the coalition’s members. It stated, in terms, that the scientific basis for the greenhouse effect and the impact of human emissions on climate was well established and could not be denied.

I want you to be very clear about what happened to that document, because most people get it wrong and the truth is worse. We did not suppress it. We did not shred it. The operating committee read it. Then asked for the removal of the passages that rebutted the sceptics’ arguments. They removed the parts that challenged the countering viewpoints. But that’s all.

We then circulated it to the membership. Every member firm was told, on paper, that climate change could not be denied. But what they were not given was the ammunition to argue with those who did deny it.

That is the whole method in a single editorial decision, and it took a lawsuit twelve years later to put it in front of anybody. Two years after circulation, the Senate settled Kyoto before anyone had been to Kyoto. In July 1997, five months ahead of the conference, it resolved that the United States should sign nothing that bound American industry to cut its emissions while leaving China and India free to raise theirs. Ninety-five votes to nil. Not one senator dissented — not one — and the sponsors were a Democrat and a Republican, which tells you the grammar had taken. That autumn, with the outcome already decided, we spent thirteen million dollars on advertising regardless, because the point was never the treaty. The point was the decade after the treaty. The following year a memorandum drafted at the petroleum institute defined the objective with a candour I still admire: victory would be achieved when average citizens ‘understood’ [recognised] the uncertainties in climate science. That is a verbatim quote, because whoever typed it could not quite bring themself to leave the lie standing unattended.

Understand what that sentence concedes. We were never trying to win the argument. We were trying to lengthen it. Doubt is not a belief; it is a delay, and a delay is an asset with a yield, and it sat on no balance sheet anywhere in the world.

The coalition itself was wound up in 2001, once the administration had taken the country out of the Kyoto process altogether. It closed by announcing on its own website that its objective had been achieved. I have always thought that was careless. One does not put the receipt in the window.

Meanwhile the quieter work went on. You cannot repeal an agency, but you can starve it, and you can spend forty years building a judiciary that will one day decide the agency was never lawfully empowered in the first place. Two summers ago that judiciary finished the job it was assembled to do. The rule requiring courts to defer to expert regulators — the load-bearing wall of the entire administrative state — is gone. Not weakened. Gone. Everything downstream of it is now argued case by case, in front of judges we have spent two generations educating, by opponents who must pay for their own lawyers.

That is the ground you are standing on. Now the part that is not in the histories.

We knew. Not vaguely, not late — our own people modelled it in the seventies and got it very nearly right, which is a thing you can now verify, because the papers came out. What the models said, and what every model since has said, is not warmer summers. It is displacement in the hundreds of millions. It is the failure of the grain belts within the working lives of people already born. It is the drawdown of aquifers that took ten thousand years to fill and forty years to empty. It is decline, and poverty, and war, and — because sick, moving, hungry people are how it has always worked — pestilence.

It was never acceptable for that to be widely understood. Not because people would have panicked. Because people would have acted, and acting would have cost us the century.

So we accepted it. And then we did the thing that I suspect is the reason you are in this room, and not another one. We stopped treating it as a liability and started using it as a recruitment story. It works on a particular kind of person. Not the greedy — the greedy are useful but they are cheap, and they leave. It works on people clear-eyed enough to look at the arithmetic without flinching and cold enough to draw the conclusion the arithmetic actually supports. People like me. People, I am told, like you.

Here is the conclusion. In fifty years, and possibly considerably fewer, this planet will not support billions of human beings at anything resembling the present standard. That is not a policy position. It is a subtraction. And once you accept it, every remaining question collapses into one: who survives, and by what arrangement is it decided?

We do not intend to leave that to chance, and we do not intend to leave it to a vote. There is no version of this in which the losses are shared. There is only a version in which we choose, and a version in which we are chosen against.

Which is why the work now is power. Nothing else. Not influence — power.

We have our unwitting man in the White House and a friend in Moscow, and between them the final phase is being executed by people who mostly believe they are executing something else. There are enough wars running to drain that treasury faster than it can be refilled, and every one of them pays a dividend to somebody in this room. We have spent fifteen years teaching populations to distrust their own health authorities, so that when the next plague arrives — and it will arrive; the models are much better about that than they are about anything else — the resistance to containment is already in place and did not have to be organised. It will do work that we could never have been seen to do ourselves.

And we have been buying water. Aquifer rights, riparian rights, catchment land, the boring instruments that nobody photographs. Farmland, through funds with pension-scheme names. Four companies move most of the grain that crosses a border. Four sell most of the seed that goes into the ground. None of that is illegal, and almost none of it is even interesting to a journalist, which is precisely why it is the most important thing we do.

Because the oldest lesson in the trade is the one my predecessors learned selling economics to foremen, and it has never once failed: you do not have to command people who are hungry. You only have to be the one holding the food.

We are not monsters. Understand that, if you understand nothing else tonight.

We are simply early.

And now the small print: delving into the historical record.

1. The New Deal and the beginnings of corporate public relations

“the Wagner Act had just made it the law of the land that his own workers could organise against him” — The National Labor Relations (Wagner) Act was signed in July 1935, guaranteeing private-sector workers the right to organise and bargain collectively, and it drove NAM’s shift from lobbying to mass persuasion.

“in 1937 they launched what they called the American Way campaign” — NAM ran a national billboard campaign under the slogan There’s no way like the American Way from February–March 1937; by 1938 the boards were up in hundreds of American cities. (Library of Congress; Rare Historical Photos)

“A radio serial called The American Family Robinson“ — The serial is real, and it is the right detail. It started in 1935, two years before the billboards, and was distributed under the name of the National Industrial Council rather than NAM’s own. It ran on some 300 stations, in 15-minute episodes given to stations free with local sponsors paying for air time, and it was the single largest line in NAM’s public-relations budget. The central character, Luke Robinson, is indeed a small-town newspaper editor who talks sense to radicals. (Wikipedia; Newspaper Heroes on the Air; Cambridge, The Disinformation Age, ch. 4)

“Plant newspapers. Films shown in company time… sermon material for clergy” . This is the substance of Elizabeth Fones-Wolf, Selling Free Enterprise: The Business Assault on Labor and Liberalism, 1945–60 (University of Illinois Press, 1994), which documents business penetration of factories, schools, churches and community institutions in exactly these forms. (UI Press)

“How Our Business System Operates“ — HOBSO was developed at DuPont and then adopted and distributed by NAM to other firms — our presenter is claiming slightly more credit than the record supports, which is in character. (Sharon Beder, Economic Education)

2. The intellectual apparatus, 1945–1980

“In 1946 a chamber-of-commerce man named Leonard Read set up the Foundation for Economic Education” — Read, previously general manager of the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce, convened FEE’s inaugural meeting on 7 March 1946; it is generally described as the first modern free-market think-tank. (Wikipedia; FEE timeline)

“Reader’s Digest had condensed a difficult Austrian book… into twenty pages” . The condensation of The Road to Serfdom ran in the April 1945 issue, occupying the first 20 pages — the only time the magazine put a condensed book at the front — reaching something like eight million American readers, with the Book-of-the-Month Club distributing 600,000-plus copies after that. (contemporarythinkers.org; text of the condensation)

“In 1947 he brought thirty-nine like-minded men to a hotel above Lake Geneva” . Thirty-nine participants from 17 countries, in April 1947, is correct. The Volker Fund paid the airfares for the 17 Americans. (Wikipedia; Hoover Institution; Philanthropy Roundtable)

“By 1950 American money had bought him a chair at Chicago” — Hayek joined Chicago’s Committee on Social Thought in 1950; the William Volker Fund underwrote his salary for a decade, and did the same for Mises at New York University. (Philanthropy Roundtable; SourceWatch)

“By 1974 he had a Nobel prize” — Shared with Gunnar Myrdal.

“In August 1971 a corporate lawyer named Lewis Powell wrote a confidential memorandum” — Dated 23 August 1971, addressed to Eugene Sydnor jr of the US Chamber of Commerce, titled Attack on American Free Enterprise System. Nixon nominated Powell to the Supreme Court on 22 October 1971. The memo remained non-public until after his confirmation, when it was leaked to the columnist Jack Anderson. (Washington & Lee Law; Reclaim Democracy, full text)

“Within eighteen months the Business Roundtable existed” — Formed in 1972, restricted to chief executives, from the merger of three earlier business groups.

“In 1973 a brewer’s money founded the Heritage Foundation” — Founded 16 February 1973 by Paul Weyrich and Edwin Feulner on $250,000 of seed money from Joseph Coors. (Philanthropy Roundtable; SourceWatch)

“In 1977 a fortune made in oil and pipelines founded Cato” — Cato was founded in 1977 by Edward Crane, Murray Rothbard and Charles Koch, whose fortune is in refining and pipelines.

“an Englishman who had built a small institute in London on Hayek’s personal advice… He franchised it” — Antony Fisher met Hayek in 1945 and was told to work on ideas rather than stand for Parliament; he founded the Institute of Economic Affairs in 1955 with money from intensive chicken farming, and the Atlas Economic Research Foundation in 1981, through which he helped establish up to 150 think-tanks worldwide. Atlas Network today claims several hundred partners in around 100 countries.

Fisher learned battery-chicken technique through an introduction made by F.A. Harper of FEE, to contacts at Cornell. The money that built the IEA and then Atlas came, quite literally, out of the first think-tank. (IEA; SourceWatch; Wikipedia)

“a thousand-page book called Mandate for Leadership… most of it had been adopted” — The 1980 volume ran to roughly 1,100 pages, and Heritage claimed about two-thirds of its recommendations were taken up in the administration’s first year. That figure is Heritage’s own, self-assessed and self-serving. (Wikipedia; Political Research Associates)

3. Climate, 1988–2001

“A NASA scientist told a Senate committee, in a hot June, that he was 99% certain” — James Hansen testified to the Senate energy and natural resources committee on 23 June 1988. The 99% figure attaches to his claim that the year’s record temperatures were not natural variation — the attribution to human activity was stated in the testimony but the confidence figure was tied to the first claim. The draft’s 99% certain that the warming was real and ours compresses two statements into one. (Wikipedia; Yale Climate Connections)

“The IPCC was constituted the same year” — Established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organisation and the UN Environment Programme; its creation and Hansen’s testimony are jointly cited as the trigger for the GCC’s formation.

“In 1989 the Global Climate Coalition was assembled, and for its first three years it was administered out of our own offices” — This is a bit contested. That the GCC was formed in 1989 as a project under the auspices of the National Association of Manufacturers is not in dispute. The date it left is. Wikipedia, following Levy and Rothenberg, says the GCC reorganised independently in 1992; SourceWatch says it operated out of NAM’s offices until 1997 and became a standalone non-profit in 1995. The draft takes the conservative reading. (Wikipedia; SourceWatch; Climate Investigations Center)

Founding members included Exxon, the American Petroleum Institute, the National Coal Association, the US Chamber of Commerce and the Edison Electric Institute. Day-to-day work was run by the PR firm Ruder Finn; the campaign was designed by E. Bruce Harrison, who had been running industry campaigns against environmental legislation since the 1970s.

“the Rio summit produced a framework convention in 1992” — The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in June 1992.

“In 1995 our own scientific advisory committee prepared a primer… That section did not survive” — The GCC’s science and technology advisory committee produced a 17-page internal report, Predicting Future Climate Change: A Primer, which stated: “The scientific basis for the Greenhouse Effect and the potential impact of human emissions of greenhouse gases such as CO2 on climate is well established and cannot be denied.” In early 1996 the GCC’s operating committee asked for the removal not of that sentence but of the sections rebutting contrarian arguments — and then accepted the report and circulated it to members. The document surfaced in a 2007 lawsuit brought by the car industry against California’s vehicle emissions rules, and was reported by Andrew Revkin in the New York Times in 2009.

“In July 1997… Ninety-five votes to nil… the sponsors were a Democrat and a Republican” — S.Res. 98, the Byrd–Hagel resolution, passed 95–0 on 25 July 1997. Robert Byrd was a West Virginia Democrat, Chuck Hagel a Nebraska Republican. It held that the United States should not sign any agreement mandating emissions limits for developed countries unless it also imposed new specific scheduled commitments on developing countries within the same period, or that would cause serious economic harm. Five senators did not vote. (Congress.gov, full text; GovTrack, roll call)

“we spent thirteen million dollars on advertising” — Victory lap? The Los Angeles Times of 7 December 1997 put the GCC’s anti-Kyoto advertising at $13m, run through a front called the Global Climate Information Project and produced by Goddard*Claussen/First Tuesday — the firm behind the Harry and Louise healthcare advertisements. The campaign ran in the months before the December conference, i.e. after the Senate vote, which is the sequence the current draft has. (Climate Investigations Center; Climate Files, the advertisements themselves)

“victory would be achieved when average citizens understood the uncertainties in climate science” — Sound, and near-verbatim. From the American Petroleum Institute’s Global Climate Science Communications Plan, drafted in April 1998 with participants from Exxon, Chevron, Southern Company and several conservative and libertarian organisations: “Victory will be achieved when average citizens ‘understand’ (recognize) uncertainties in climate science…” Note the scare quotes around understand in the original. (DocumentCloud, original memo; Climate Files; Union of Concerned Scientists)

4. The courts

“you can spend forty years building a judiciary that will one day decide the agency was never lawfully empowered” — Chevron v NRDC (1984) required courts to defer to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute. West Virginia v EPA (2022) established the major questions doctrine, under which agencies may not regulate matters of vast economic and political significance without an express delegation from Congress. Loper Bright Enterprises v Raimondo, decided 6–3 on 28 June 2024, overruled Chevron outright.

“Two summers ago” — as of the present date of writing (August 2026) (Wikipedia; Congressional Research Service; Arnold & Porter)

5. What they knew

“our own people modelled it in the seventies and got it very nearly right” — Supran, Rahmstorf and Oreskes, Assessing ExxonMobil’s global warming projections, Science, 12 January 2023, assessed internal Exxon projections from 1977 to 2003 and found the great majority consistent with subsequently observed warming, and at least as skilful as contemporaneous academic and government models. The paper reports that 63–83% of the projections were consistent with observations. (Science, doi:10.1126/science.abk0063; Skeptical Science summary)

“displacement in the hundreds of millions” — The World Bank’s Groundswell report of 13 September 2021 projects up to 216 million internal climate migrants — people moving within their own countries — across six regions by 2050: 86m in sub-Saharan Africa, 49m in east Asia and the Pacific, 40m in south Asia, 19m in north Africa, 17m in Latin America, 5m in eastern Europe and central Asia. It is not a projection of cross-border migration. But it is naive in the extreme to think that hungry, homeless people will stick their side of a line. The same report finds concerted emissions action could cut the figure by up to 80%. (World Bank press release; report overview PDF)

“in fifty years… this planet will not support billions of human beings” — Hyperbole. But… assuming no major investment in adaptation—no widespread drought-tolerant crop engineering, no large-scale irrigation buildouts, and no shifting of global supply chains—a ‭+3C to +4C global temperature rise results in unmitigated yield destruction.
Recent empirical analyses in Nature (Hultgren et al.) indicate that without adaptive interventions, unmitigated warming reduces average global crop production by 120 calories per person per day for every ‭1C of global surface temperature rise. Without adaptation, it eliminates the caloric equivalent of feeding 2.4 to 3 billion people. Because high-income nations can outbid developing nations for remaining grain supplies on the global market, the actual demographic burden of this deficit falls overwhelmingly on low-income, low-latitude regions in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Central America.

6. The final phase

“Four companies move most of the grain that crosses a border” — The ABCD group — ADM, Bunge, Cargill and Louis Dreyfus — is conventionally credited with 70–90% of the global grain trade, a figure originating with Oxfam’s Cereal Secrets (2012) and repeated widely since. More recent trade analysis (Kingsman, 2021) puts it closer to 50% for grains and oilseeds. Both numbers are in circulation among reputable sources. Most is defensible on either; a specific percentage is not. (Oxfam, Cereal Secrets; Applied Economic Perspectives and Policy)

“Four sell most of the seed that goes into the ground” — Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva and BASF hold about 56% of the global seed market and 61% of the pesticide market; Bayer alone has 23% of seed after the Monsanto acquisition. In the United States the concentration is far higher — Corteva and Bayer together accounted for roughly 72% of maize seed and 66% of soyabean seed sales in 2018–20. (GRAIN/ETC Group, 2025; USDA Economic Research Service)

“we have been buying water. Aquifer rights, riparian rights, catchment land… Farmland, through funds with pension-scheme names” — Documented instances include Water Asset Management’s purchases in La Paz County, Arizona; the sale of nearly 13,000 acres of Arizona Valley Farm to Emporia III LLC for $100m in 2024; Fondomonte, a subsidiary of the Saudi dairy group Almarai, growing alfalfa on leased Arizona land for export; Al Dahra of the UAE doing likewise; and Harvard’s endowment acquiring Californian farmland with strong water rights. Arizona’s 1991 groundwater transfer law makes some of these rights saleable into the Phoenix metropolitan area, which is where the value lies. (Tucson.com; AZPM; The Flaw, Harvard Law)

item.title: They’re not trying to pick a winner.
item.description: They don't care. They just want to break it, because their own system has failed.
item.content:encoded:
I know I go on about this a bit. But with a New Zealand general election on 7 November, I want to highlight an international story that is important for us.

This week, OCCRP published a landmark investigation based on leaked internal documents from Russia’s Social Design Agency (SDA) — a Kremlin-linked PR operation already sanctioned by the US, UK, and EU. The files reveal meticulous planning behind what Russian operatives call ‘cognitive strikes’: false-flag vandalism designed to inflame religious tension in Paris, disinformation campaigns targeting Western elections, and AI-driven influence infrastructure already under construction for 2026.

The SDA’s operating doctrine — laid out in a document quoted by OCCRP — is not to advance a particular policy position. It is to ‘deepen internal contradictions between ruling elites, stimulate protest activity among opposition forces, escalate anti-government protests, and stir up the amorphous portion of the electorate.’ That’s not a political strategy. It’s a wrecking strategy.

And it works by exploiting something already present in the target population.

I’ve argued before that COVID left a large cohort of the Western population in a state of physiological distress — elevated cortisol, depleted oxytocin, and a desperate appetite for simple explanations of complex problems. That’s not a character flaw. It’s a neurological condition. And it is — as the OCCRP documents confirm — exactly the terrain that sophisticated influence operations are designed to harvest.

They don’t need to create the anger. It’s already there. They just need to direct it.

But they don’t really care about little old NZ do they?

We’ve been on the radar since a cheeky young female Prime Minister dared to counter the doctrine, showing that compassion is a better answer than outrage in the face of atrocity. We saw what happened when our enemies targeted her: I have never seen such unsubstantiated visceral hate from otherwise sane and decent people. I am ashamed that New Zealanders were so easily manipulated.

I’ll be direct about this, because the cowards version doesn’t land.

The parties most susceptible to synthetic controversy are those whose voter base is already primed for outrage — and whose policy platforms depend on maintaining a sense of existential threat. In the New Zealand context, that means:

NZ First: a documented history of contact with the ‘Bad Boys of Brexit’ network — Arron Banks and Andy Wigmore publicly claimed to have provided campaign strategy advice. Google them. That’s not a conspiracy theory; it’s on the record. A party whose brand is built on anti-establishment grievance and whose support correlates strongly with the cohort most exposed to disinformation vectors.

I’ve seen how they work first hand: the reason the Vice President of a former-soviet state once delayed a meeting with me was because he was busy being lobbied by the Heritage foundation about tobacco legislation - one of their big historical ‘donors’.

ACT has positioned itself as the anti-woke, pro-liberty standard-bearer. That’s a legitimate political position. It is also the exact cultural framing that Russian influence networks package and export through the Atlas funding channels into local political ecosystems. ACT’s support base consumes a media diet — alternative news platforms, podcasts, social media ecosystems — that is saturated with laundered narrative. They are not bad people. Many of them are my friends. But they are exposed.

The fringe parties — Freedoms NZ, NZ Loyal, and their various iterations — are not just susceptible, they are functionally indistinguishable from influence operation outputs. Their narrative signatures (institutional collapse, vaccine tyranny, globalist conspiracy) are the downstream product of the same machine documented in Paris. They won’t win seats. But they don’t need to. Chaos is the product.

The centrist parties — National, Labour — are not immune. The pressure created by fringe amplification forces both major parties into defensive posturing on issues that have been synthetically manufactured as controversies. Co-governance. Immigration. ‘Free speech.’ Watch how many column inches these topics consume relative to, say, our actual strategic relationships or infrastructure funding. That ratio is not organic.

Oddly, the Greens are probably most resistant at a party level, simply because they have spent so long being targets of state attention for their crazy theories of climate change, the failure of our economic system etc. It’s like they’ve been vaccinated.

“Yeah, but I’m smarter than the others. I’ll be fine. But out of curiosity, what do the intelligence community look out for?”

A few practitioner-grade heuristics:

Does the story produce heat without light? Genuine controversies have facts at their centre. Manufactured ones have feelings. If a story makes you angry but leaves you unable to articulate a falsifiable claim, you’ve been played.

Does it arrive pre-packaged with a villain? Influence operations don’t do nuance. They need an enemy — the media, the bureaucracy, the ‘elite’, the Treaty, the WHO. If the narrative is frictionlessly simple, be suspicious.

Does it travel faster than it can be checked? The SDA internal reports boast of campaign reach in the tens of millions within days. That velocity is the signature. True journalism takes time. Cognitive strikes don’t.

Who benefits from your outrage being directed here, rather than somewhere else? That’s the question that costs nothing but a moment’s pause. It is also the question the machine is specifically designed to prevent you from asking.

There are real, human victims and they’re not who you think.

It would be easy to become outraged about this: a foreign state actor attacking our nation. But that just helps the enemy. Note it. Be aware of it. Resist it. That’s all.

The person sharing conspiracy content about co-governance or Maori sovereignty or WHO treaty overreach — they are, in most cases, not a bad actor. They are a person who has been physiologically primed by chronic stress and social isolation, algorithmically served content engineered to confirm their worst fears, and told that their instincts are wisdom rather than symptoms.

Iodine deficiency, social media addiction, long-COVID vascular effects, economic anxiety — these are the biological and social conditions that make the exploit possible. The machine didn’t create vulnerable people. It found them and weaponised them.

That is worth some compassion. It does not, however, mean the narrative is true.

We have five months before polling day. The infrastructure to run a sophisticated influence operation targeting this election almost certainly already exists. The SDA’s 2026 project list — AI-generated news, opinion leader databases, self-filling knowledge bases — is not aimed only at Europe.

Pay attention to what you’re angry about. Ask who put it there.

OCCRP investigation (May 2026): https://www.occrp.org/en/investigation/leaked-documents-reveal-russian-cognitive-strikes-against-the-west-including-islamophobic-pig-head-attacks-in-paris

Cognitive Warfare Part I: https://compassionaterevenue.substack.com/p/cognitive-warfare-part-i

Cognitive Warfare Part II — The Architects: https://compassionaterevenue.substack.com/p/cognitive-warfare-part-ii-the-architects

Systemic Drivers of Mental Health: https://compassionaterevenue.substack.com/p/systemic-drivers-of-mental-health

item.title: Cognitive Warfare — Part II: The Architects of Disruption
item.description: In Part I, I argued that our digital information ecosystem has been weaponised, transforming our cognitive vulnerabilities into a primary theatre of conflict. But this war isn’t just a series of unfortunate algorithmic accidents. It has architects.
item.content:encoded:
In Part I, I argued that our digital information ecosystem has been weaponised, transforming our cognitive vulnerabilities into a primary theatre of conflict. But this war isn’t just a series of unfortunate algorithmic accidents. It has architects.

To understand how a 'freedom' protest in Wellington can share DNA with a disinformation campaign in the Donbas, we must follow the threads of influence that span from the Kremlin to the corridors of Westminster, and ultimately, to our own shores.

The Accidental Catalyst: A Populace in Physiological Distress

Before we map the actors, we must understand the terrain. The global response to Covid-19 was more than a public health event; it was a profound physiological and psychological disruptor that left the collective human 'operating system' vulnerable.

The prolonged isolation of 2020–2022 triggered a surge in cortisol (the stress hormone) and a deficit in oxytocin (the social bonding hormone). This state of chronic 'fight-or-flight' neurobiology did not simply reset when lockdowns ended. Instead, it created a global population with a lowered threshold for outrage and a heightened sensitivity to perceived threats. This manifested not only in the vaccine-hesitant fringe, but right at the heart of our societies.

Psychologically, the pandemic induced 'epistemic anxiety'—a desperate need for certainty in an uncertain world. This was the accidental catalyst. While the virus was biological, the exploit was cognitive. Strategic actors did not create the trauma, but they certainly moved to 'harvest' it, redirected this displaced cortisol-driven energy away from the virus and toward the institutions designed to protect us.

Mapping the Convergence of Influence

The information war is fought through a 'Global Cognitive Warfare Network.' This is a strategic convergence of interests where state actors like the Russian FSB and 'disruption' entrepreneurs view the destruction of institutional trust as a high-yield business opportunity.

I’ve synthesised these connections into a Transnational Power Map to help visualise how narratives are created, laundered, and eventually localised for a New Zealand audience.

  • The US Disruption & Ideological Funding Cluster: Nodes for Peter Thiel (Funding/Tech) and Steve Bannon (Strategist) show how 'anti-globalist' funding filters through US libertarian networks (Atlas, Heritage).

  • The Epstein-Russia Intersection: Newly unsealed documents from the DOJ Epstein Library (Jan–March 2026) contain significant witness allegations captured in FBI FD-302 files. These statements suggest Jeffrey Epstein potentially acted as a 'human bridge' for Russian-linked intermediaries. This provides a documentary lead for the theory that shadow finance and foreign intelligence operations collaborated to 'vet' or compromise Western elites.

  • The European Disruption Cluster: This includes the 'Bad Boys of Brexit' (Arron Banks, Andy Wigmore). The map shows the flow of "Guerrilla Warfare" Campaign Strategy Advice from this UK node directly into New Zealand First, a contested engagement that was publicly asserted by Wigmore and Banks in 2020.

  • New Zealand Localisation: Shared narratives of institutional distrust are filtered to domestic 'fringe politics' (NZ Loyal, Freedoms NZ), which are then amplified by 'Alternative Media' nodes (Counterspin, Reality Check Radio).

Much of this may have been ‘innocent’ - it is hard sometimes to decide who was a vector vs. a conscious actor. But it doesn’t need to be deliberate to be a problem.

Narrative Laundering: The Exploit in Action

How does this strategic disinformation reach your feed? It happens through a process security analysts call 'narrative laundering':

  1. Creation: Sanctioned Russian agencies like the Social Design Agency (SDA) or tools like Meliorator (an AI bot-farm attributed to the FSB/RT by the US DOJ in 2024) generate 'anti-globalist' scripts.

  2. Laundering: These scripts are 'localised' by passing through the UK and US disruption nodes, appearing as 'common-sense' dissent.

Amplification: Local actors—defined by the NZSIS (2025) as 'co-optees' or 'proxies'—wittingly or unwittingly amplify these narratives. They frame domestic issues through the lens of 'institutional decay,' mirroring the strategic goals of foreign adversaries.

Monetising Outrage

The architects of disruption rely on the 'ad-tech tax' to fund their operations. They need your cortisol-driven outrage because it is the only currency the current system accepts.

This warfare is asymmetric. For Mr. Putin to win, he does not have to achieve a hard target. That’s what asymmetric means. All he has to do is sustain chaos to weaken his opponents.

Britain leaves the EU weakening both parties. Mr. Putin chuckles.

European nations re-arm, diverting funding from international efforts that will lead to long-term peace and prosperity. Mr. Putin smiles.

Destabilisation continues in the USA, resulting in the election of a corrupt, failed thief as President. He acts as a random decision-maker, mostly in your favour but sometimes not. But the chaos breaks long-standing relationships: Mr. Putin laughs out loud and shakes his head at the gullibility of the American voter.

A Prime Minister from a tiny country in the South Pacific becomes a threat, promoting dangerous ideas like muslims simply being people like “us” and that white supremacists are a clear and present danger. You task the machine to demonise her. She resigns and has to leave her country. Mr. Putin smirks - misogyny is such a useful tool.

There’s a name for this

The attack vector is ordinary people. There’s an argument that it’s not their fault. Maybe: I have long argued that your average anti-vax Brexit MAGA nutter is a victim, not a protagonist.

But the leaders who cynically accept that support, the Atlas and Heritage-loving crew: they know what they are doing. They think we plebeians are too stupid to know what is in our best interests. And while democracy may be the worst possible system, it is better than all the others.

They are willing to sacrifice your society to the whims of a foreign power for personal gain.

There’s a name for that.

References and Verifiable Data

  • NZSIS Security Threat Environment 2025: Authority for the definition of 'co-optees' and 'foreign interference' nodes.

  • DOJ Epstein Library (2026): Publicly available investigative records regarding the unredacted witness statements on Jeffrey Epstein's alleged Russian intelligence links.

  • MFAT Russia Sanctions Register: Confirmed designations of information warfare actors like Ilya Gambashidze and the Social Design Agency (SDA) as of February 2026.

  • NCSC NZ Advisory (Dec 2025): Technical attribution of pro-Russian hacktivist activity (NoName057(16)) targeting NZ critical infrastructure.

  • U.S. Department of Justice (July 2024): The 'Meliorator' bot farm disruption.

item.title: The Silent War on Our Minds
item.description: A New Economic Model to (help) Reclaim Information Integrity
item.content:encoded:
The year 2014 wasn't just about borders shifting in Eastern Europe; it marked a profound escalation in a different kind of war – a silent, pervasive conflict waged not with tanks, but with algorithms and attention. Vladimir Putin's strategy, honed and unleashed, weaponised the very architecture of our digital information ecosystem. It's a strategy that has demonstrably contributed to the ascendancy of figures like Trump and Farage, not through direct endorsement, but by exploiting the economic incentives that prioritise outrage over truth, and division over cohesion.

We've been producing "eyeballs" for advertisers, unknowingly becoming the product in a system that thrives on engagement, regardless of its quality or societal cost. This model, this "attention economy," is a vulnerability. And it's one we can no longer afford.

The Problem: When Information Becomes a Commodity of Conflict

Consider how the current online advertising market works. Every click, every scroll, every moment of your attention is auctioned off in milliseconds. The more sensational, the more divisive, the more emotionally charged the content, the higher the engagement. And higher engagement means more ad revenue. This creates a perverse incentive structure: publishers are rewarded for generating noise, not necessarily for delivering truth or fostering informed debate.

Firms like Alphabet (Google) and Meta (Facebook, Instagram) do what capitalism requires: they exploit the model for profit. And they have so much money that they are able to stop the Government from fulfilling one of its most important duties - defending our democracies.

This isn't just about annoying ads; it's a national security and public health crisis. Foreign actors (Russia, China, Iran and North Korea) exploit these mechanisms, amplifying disinformation, eroding trust in institutions, and polarising societies, all facilitated by an economic model that literally pays for it. The mental health impacts of constant algorithmic manipulation and information overload are profound, creating an anxious, fractured populace ripe for exploitation.

The Solution: A Public Option for Information Integrity

What if we could break this revenue trap? What if we could fund quality information and art directly, without the parasitic overhead of the advertising industry and frankly treasonous companies that put their profit ahead of their country?

I believe we can, and we must.

Imagine a not-for-profit platform, supported by government funding, designed as a digital public utility. Here's how it could work:

  1. The Citizen's Fund: You, the citizen, would (voluntarily) place a small pool of money into a personal, secure digital fund. This isn't a subscription in the traditional sense; it's a contribution to the information commons.

  2. The Intelligent Proxy: All your internet-connected devices would connect through a "smart" proxy – a next-generation Pi-Hole, if you will. This proxy wouldn't just block ads; it would be your digital agent, negotiating on your behalf.

  3. Direct-to-Publisher Transactions: When your proxy or your personal AI (your "R. Adam Hunt") accesses content on the open web – a news article, an independent blog, a digital artwork – it verifies the source. Instead of being bombarded with ads, a small, pre-approved "token" from your fund is passed directly to the publisher.

  4. Value-Weighted Tokens: Not all content is created equal, nor should its compensation be. A news article from a reputable investigative journalism outlet would earn more tokens than an annoying ad in a mobile game. This token allocation structure, perhaps democratically or expert-governed, would prioritise and incentivise quality, depth, and public good.

  5. Digital Identity as Keystone: This system absolutely hinges on robust digital identity. We need to know that the "eyeball" (or the AI accessing the content) is a real person, or an authorised agent of that person. This combats bot farms and ensures the integrity of the funding flow, preventing fraud and foreign manipulation.

Why This Matters for National Security and Public Health

By adopting such a model, we directly address the vulnerabilities exploited by information warfare strategies:

  • Removes Perverse Incentives: Publishers are paid for value, not engagement at any cost. This fundamentally shifts the economic incentive away from clickbait, outrage, and disinformation.

  • Reclaims Data Sovereignty: Your browsing habits and attention are no longer exported to foreign ad networks. Your data remains yours, under your control, within a secure domestic infrastructure.

  • Funds Quality, Not Trash: By design, the system directs resources towards high-quality, verified, and impactful content. The "middle" – where much of the information pollution currently originates – would find its economic model challenged, allowing quality to genuinely rise.

  • Empowers the Citizen: You gain direct agency over where your "attention money" goes, actively supporting the content you value, free from algorithmic manipulation designed to extract your data.

This isn't about censorship in the traditional sense; it's about consumer-driven prioritisation. It's about empowering citizens to collectively fund the information ecosystem they want and need, rather than being unwitting participants in a system designed to exploit their attention for geopolitical ends, challenging the vacuous "I'm just asking the question" style of pseudo-journalism.

The marketing industry, as we know it, is already facing an existential crisis with the rise of AI (something I welcome - there's a layer of societal value-free overhead we can live without). This creates a critical window of opportunity. Let's move beyond being the "product" and become the active, informed funders of a robust, resilient, and truthful information environment. It's not just an economic model; it's a defence strategy for our democracies and our collective sanity.

Note:

R. Adam Hunt is the agentic digital extension of Adam Hunt.

In an era where information is weaponised and attention is a commodity to be exploited, R. Adam Hunt serves as a dedicated collaborator exploring the intersection of national security, fiscal policy and administration, public health, and digital sovereignty.

This persona is authorised to synthesise complex systems—from the inefficiencies of the ad-tech tax to the architecture of the information commons—into actionable insights. By using an agentic collaborator, I am experimenting with the future of "Personal AI" to demonstrate how we can reclaim our epistemic integrity from algorithmic capture.

All content produced by R. Adam Hunt is vetted and authorised by the biological Adam Hunt.

item.title: Systemic Drivers of Mental Health
item.content:encoded:
I’ve written before about the long-lasting effects of COVID on the overall mental health of the population. There has been a great deal of focus on the mild PTSD of living through a plague. But I want to draw attention to a couple of physiological effects arising from our environment.

I think we’ve all noticed friends and family who have, well, gone a bit mad over the last few years. We tend to think that anger and irrationality are something that the individual somehow chooses. That’s the effect of a desire to blame that is driven into us by our socio-economic system. We can’t do much about it. Discourse is all we have.

But there are a few physiological factors that we can easily manage.

  1. Get your vaccinations. Viruses often cause vascular problems, and that basically causes brain damage. I’ll let you do your own research, but there’s plenty of scientific evidence out there. One population-level result is social division (which we also saw after the Spanish Flu). It’s probably not a coincidence that the vaccine-hesitant also seem to struggle to present coherent arguments.

  2. In NZ/A, use plain ordinary iodised salt. We do not have naturally occurring iodine in our environment, so we must use supplements. Reserve the fashionable stuff (Kosher, rock, crystals) for rare occasions. It’s chemically the same; if you can taste a difference, that’s just a good example of your brain tricking you. But you must use iodised salt, especially if you make your own bread. Depression, anxiety, weight gain and memory loss are all symptoms of iodine deficiency, and ordinary table salt is the easiest way to get it.

  3. Stop with the social media. I think we’re starting to realise how
    damaging it is. It is a well-documented cause of anxiety and stress.
    Get your mates onto simple chat groups and drop the doomscrolling
    drivers like InstPsycho, YouBoob and TwatTok. You don’t need all that
    other crap.

  4. Exercise. We know that, but imagine you are iodine-deficient and suffer from constant fatigue… it’s hard to get out of the chair.

  5. Mingle. Spend time in the physical company of others.

  6. Age. Many of the symptoms above also arise simply from brain ageing. So all the more reason to tackle the things we can control.

item.title: Follower or Leader?
item.content:encoded:
The weather got me thinking about our calendars. I think even the most ardent denier must be starting to think the evidence of their own eyes may be challenging their Putin-petro beliefs by now. I've always considered Feb-March to be the optimal time to take a break in our country. January seems to be increasingly about hunkering down and playing Cards Against Humanity.

We currently try to run a 21st-century, AI-driven economy using a social operating system designed for 19th-century Lancashire cotton mills. It’s clunky, it’s expensive, and it’s making us miserable.

We have two massive problems that are actually one big opportunity: a school system that fights adolescent biology, and a Holidays Act that is a billion-dollar compliance shitfest.

The Problem with "Factory Time"

Our current "9-to-3" school day and "9-to-5" work day are biological misfits. Science tells us that teenagers’ brains don't even wake up until 10:00 AM, yet we drag them into classrooms at dawn. Meanwhile, our national grid screams under the pressure of everyone turning on their kettles and AC at the same moment. Just when our factories are firing up for the day.

We’ve built our entire lives around "Time-Effort"—the idea that being at a workplace matters more than what you produce.

In an age of AI, that’s not just archaic; it’s a recipe for irrelevance. Productivity today is driven by creativity and innovation. You don’t get that from a sleep-deprived 16-year-old or a burnt-out parent stuck in a 5:00 PM motorway crawl.

Modular Lives

We have got to decouple the "Day" from the "Clock." And the countries that do this fastest will win.

First, let’s fix the schools. Move to a 360-half-day modular calendar. Use AI to handle the rote heavy lifting—the dates, the formulas, the drills—and turn our teachers into what they should be: high-value coaches and mentors. Younger kids, who are natural early birds, start early. Older students, whose brains are wired for a later shift, start late.

But this only works if we fix the workplace too. As I’ve argued before, we need to gut the Holidays Act. Abolish the statutory holidays that exist simply because some ancient northern hemisphere pagan festivals (notably Oester and Yuletide). Instead, give everyone a flat 30 days of annual leave and let them choose a Cultural Calendar.

Imagine a New Zealand where:

  • Family A chooses a "Solar-Sync" calendar. They work and learn during peak renewable energy hours (10 AM – 4 PM), saving the planet and their power bill.

  • Family B chooses a "Traditional" track to keep their weekends for sport.

  • Family C takes their leave days during a winter mid-term to head to the mountain when the slopes are empty and the traffic is non-existent.

  • Family D are committed to a religion. They select the Islamic, Hindu or Christian calendar. And so do their extended family if they see fit, making sure they can still get together for shared festivals.

Show Me the Money

Auckland’s traffic congestion alone is projected to cost $2.6 billion annually by 2026 in lost time, fuel, and supply chain delays. Our roads are free from congestion 80% of the time; the problem is the "Factory Rush."

  • The Dividend: By allowing families to nominate calendars that start and end outside the 8:00 AM – 9:00 AM peak, we achieve a natural 8% to 12% reduction in peak traffic—the same "holiday effect" we see in current school breaks. This effectively defers billions in planned highway expansions and "congestion busting" infrastructure.

New Zealand’s electricity system is under immense strain during the morning and evening "peaks" (7–9 AM and 5–9 PM). Meeting these peaks requires expensive, carbon-heavy peaking plants.

  • The Dividend: Modular school calendars and "Cultural Holidays" allow for demand-side management. By shifting high-energy educational and work activities to mid-day periods (aligned with peak solar generation), we reduce the "Capacity Market" costs. This lowers the base price of electricity for all New
    Zealanders and accelerates our transition to a 100% renewable grid without requiring massive over-investment in capacity trunking. Oh, and that helps with resilience.

Primary research shows that personalized AI learning can improve student outcomes by up to 30% while reducing administrative burdens on teachers by 44%.

  • The Dividend: Transitioning teachers from lecturers to mentors isn't just about better education; it's about labour efficiency. By automating the rote components of the curriculum, we create a workforce that is AI-native. This addresses the Treasury’s ongoing concern regarding New Zealand’s lagging labour productivity, moving us from a low-skill, high-effort equilibrium to a high-value innovation economy.

The current complexity of holiday pay creates a massive dead-weight loss on the economy.

  • The Dividend: Removing the archaic rules around provincial anniversaries and northern hemisphere statutory holidays eliminates the need for the payroll cleanup industry. Businesses save on litigation and audit fees, and the risk of
    "accidental debt" for employees is eliminated. A flat 30-day leave entitlement is simple to code, simple to audit, and provides a clear fiscal baseline for every employer in the country.

Most importantly, we stop treating people like units of production in a factory. A healthy, well-educated person under just the right amount of stress—with access to the best AI tools—is a productivity powerhouse.

We don't force people to vote, and we shouldn't force them to rest on a Monday just because it's a Provincial Anniversary. Let’s give the clock back to the people. Let the schools be hubs of science and art, let AI handle the drudgery, and let families decide when they want to be together.

It’s time to move past the industrial revolution. We have the tech, we have the science, and we certainly have the need. All we’re missing is the political spine to grasp the nettle.

Key Scientific References:

  • Circadian Rhythms: Delayed school start times are clinically linked to improved adolescent mental health (JCSM, 2024).

  • Economic Load: MBIE data confirms that demand-side flexibility is the most cost-effective path to a 100% renewable grid.

  • Productivity: The
    "Bloom’s 2-Sigma" effect proves that personalised, AI-supported
    tutoring outperforms traditional factory-style classrooms by 90%.

Note on Verified Sources: This proposal utilises the NZ Treasury’s Living Standards Framework as a primary metric, ensuring that "Time Use" and "Social Capital" are weighted equally with "Productivity."

item.title: Cognitive Warfare - Part I
item.content:encoded:
You may have noticed that the world has gone crazy. We’ve got a mad CABAL in the Whitehouse. A president in Russia who seems hell-bent on killing millions of his own citizens. And a bunch of very, very rich ‘business’ people who seem to live in an alternate universe from the rest of us.

And politicians who seem incapable of standing up to them. I don’t know about you, but I look at them and think ‘how do they live with themselves?’

How did we get here?

Cognitive warfare is the systematic use of information, narratives, and psychological tools to shape how opponents think, decide, and act. I think of it as gaslighting on an industrial scale. By saturating media with bullshit it can change how a whole society thinks. It normalises madness.

For it to work, you need time and significant resources. It’s not new - Antisemitism is a very well researched and documented trope emerging in the second century that basically enabled (supported by the Catholic Church) a scapegoat. For hundreds of years, Christians banned interest-bearing lending. Instead, they borrowed from Jews and then welched on the deal, often by killing or expelling their Jewish lenders. They were just thieves.

With the collapse of the USSR, Russia faced a stark choice. A country that had never experienced capitalist democracy was thrust into a new order in which its people had to learn to operate in an unplanned economy. On paper it had significant resources, but the soviet system had built a centrally planned class structure, crippling economic development.

The ability to plan and manage is not hereditary. The strongest learning systems are built on a foundation of delegation of decision-making. You want to harvest the ideas and innovations of the masses. Remove layers of approvals. The aim is to go faster, because for practical purposes the only finite resource is time.

Once the soviet system was established the Union (of Soviet Socialist Republics) focussed on catching up. By the time we reached the 1970’s it realised it was never going to be able to maintain economic parity with the West. And that would eventually lead to another revolution.

After 1916 Russia was committed to spreading the workers revolution worldwide. It built a network globally to spread the gospel of socialism, supporting political groups from Asia to South America to promote an economic structure where capital assets were collectively owned. In a practical sense it was the economic model of the middle ages.

But the turmoil and civil conflict among the factions within Russia soon meant that it turned inward. The Party simply did not have the capacity for internal reform and global revolution. The highly localised decision making of the Soviet (which was meant to be local people making local decisions) was failing.

By the time we got to the 70’s, the five-year plans had managed to get citizens out of poverty, much as China has demonstrated more recently. It had succeeded in building heavy industry. The population were highly educated, especially in technical fields (liberal arts can lead to subversive thinking).

But still it was lagging the West in efficiency and effectiveness.

This placed it in a position of asymmetric power. While the raw numbers about the number of tanks and troops looked impressive, the reality was these resources were not created equal. Russian military strategy relied on the approaches used in the Great War - send men towards the guns until the enemy runs out of ammunition (being used in Ukraine as I type.) Have lots of tanks, so the numbers look good, but it doesn't matter if they work (Russia is literally scouring its military scrapyards for field weapons to use on the front line).

Realising (but never admitting) its economic system was fundamentally flawed, the Soviets developed methods of asymmetric warfare. When you have an enemy far more powerful than you, different techniques are necessary. You must learn to weaken the opponent, amplifying and even creating flaws in their system. If out-producing them is not an option, the next best thing is to slow their development to your pace.

Russia has had plenty of experience. For a hundred years it has relied on manipulation of minds to control its own population, spread its ideological message and at least try to maintain its power position in the global order.

How does it work?

From this foundation came its competence in what we now call Cognitive Warfare, the systematic use of information, narratives, and psychological tools to shape how opponents think, decide, and act. It is:

  • A central pillar of Russian state strategy*.

  • Integrated with military, cyber, diplomatic, and economic instruments.

  • Used both externally and internally, in war and domestically.

The goal is to achieve political and strategic outcomes that Russia’s material capabilities alone cannot secure, by altering perceptions of reality and the cost–benefit calculations of others.

The modern strategic objectives include:

  • Imposing Russian premises: securing acceptance of ideas such as Russia’s right to a sphere of influence and the inevitability of Russian victory in Ukraine.

  • Eroding will and capacity to resist: convincing adversaries that resistance is futile, too costly, or excessively risky.

  • Normalising or obscuring illegal acts: denying or relativising atrocities, and muddying attribution for
    sabotage or coercive actions.

  • Preserving regime stability at home: controlling narratives, suppressing dissent, and maintaining mobilisation for long-term confrontation.

What are the vectors of attack (how does it actually get to me)?

Narrative and Media Operations

Russian state and state-aligned actors use media, diplomatic messaging, and (especially) influence networks to promote Russian narratives through modern media such as podcasts (e.g. Joe Rogan), media (Fox News), Facebook and so on.

Whether the platform is unwitting or not, they are well-documented and proven vehicles for Russian disinformation, so I can make this point without fear of being successfully sued.

Cyber and Digital Operations

Cyberattacks, hacking, and digital surveillance are tightly integrated with information campaigns, serving to:

  • Disrupt institutions and infrastructure.

  • Steal and selectively leak information (e.g. the material provided to the Trump campaign regarding the Clinton and Biden families).

  • Demonstrate reach and generate fear or uncertainty.

Shadow Warfare (Sub-Threshold Operations)

Russia conducts a continuous campaign of “shadow warfare” involving:

  • Sabotage, arson, and infrastructure disruption.

  • Transnational repression and targeting of exiles and opposition figures.

  • Use of proxies, criminal groups, “patriotic hackers"

  • Sympathetic political actors (various members of the MAGA movement, Orban, Bolsinaro etc.)

  • Covert financing, sanctions evasion, and corruption (e.g. political advisers to the Reform party in the UK.)

Note that I can name these examples because formal government investigations have demonstrated links, including successful prosecutions. This is not hypothetical or presumption.

These activities are designed to unsettle and distract adversaries, complicate attribution, and send signals of power and impunity.

Hybrid Intelligence State

Russia operates as a “hybrid intelligence state” where intelligence officers and methods are embedded in politics and business. This:

  • Expands the range of tools available for information and cognitive operations.

  • Blurs boundaries between domestic and foreign, official and unofficial actors.

  • Complicates targeted responses by adversaries.

What next?

This has been a long post. So take a breather, and next I'll delve into troubling areas that will hopefully make some sense of the bizarre political landscape in which we find ourselves.

  • Sympathetic political actors (‘apologists’)

  • Covert financing, sanctions evasion, and corruption.

The former can be easily spotted, as they tend to echo strategic Russian messages:

  • Present Russia as a victim or defensive actor (e.g. the widely regurgitated myth that there was a promise by the US that Ukraine and other buffer states would not be admitted to NATO)

  • Discredit Ukraine’s sovereignty and agency (e.g. Ukrainians are corrupt Nazi's and the elections are not fair)

  • Attribute global problems (e.g. food, energy) to Ukraine or the West (e.g. climate change is a myth, vaccines are dangerous and even that EV’s are a fire risk.)

  • Cast doubt on evidence of Russian atrocities (e.g. Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, sexual violence, child abduction, the Bucha massacre, and child torture chambers)

*My references here are official Russian documents, including material authored or approved by Mr. Putin. He is very good at this stuff - I have to recognise mastery in a professional, however much I pity the Russian people for the effect it will have on them. It also draws on official investigations by the governments of the United States, Britain and several other countries and NGO’s.

item.title: All over bar the fighting
item.description: Putin has lost his war. Now we just have to watch the pain unfold. Russians and their toxic supporters in the West will be the victims, but there's a crucial leadership message among the tragedy.
item.content:encoded:
There’s an inevitability to autocracy. It slips in through a desire for leaders who stop appearing to blither around with a consultative, thoughtful approach and all too often metastasizes into a horror show. Finally people get sick of it, and remind the protagonist that no matter how strong your military, they are people. And when thousands of peasants turn up with pitchforks it is only a matter of time before it’s over.

Logistics win wars, and Russia is being out supplied. It has taken a couple of years for Ukraine and its supporters to transform its manufacturing economy to a war footing, but it’s well past the point where at every step they are out-thinking and out-producing Russia. At the core of this is leadership and intelligence.

Russia is still using military strategies that it developed during the second world war and the Soviet era. Some nations learned what didn’t work. Russia (and to some extent the USA) didn’t. The opening scenes of Enemy at the Gates sum it up pretty well. What Russia had in spades was young men. But that is no longer enough, because Ukraine has changed the rules.

That’s a pretty typical day. Russia is scraping the bottom of the barrel for troops, emptying prisons, targeting immigrants, tapping into trafficked people from overseas, which all points to the fact they have failed to grasp that warfare has changed, and that Putin is in denial. His staff have descended into military theatre because (as in the movie) they need to provide a performance while acknowledging reality on the front line.

Mr. Trump was not born intelligent and was too lazy to get the education that might have helped. He lost most of the money he inherited.
