He’s a coward - daddy and crooked doctors got him 6 deferments from the draft. He’s a thief, stealing millions off the ordinary subcontractors (builders, electricians, plumbers and plasterers) who worked on his white elephant developments. He was an easy mark for Putin, who gained extra leverage by the mass targeting of bullies and sociopaths to recruit a base.

But still none of this will work, because both are cynics about what motivates people.

This shows by the efforts of the people of the west to support the people of Ukraine. A bunch of decent people flooding to provide support outside government channels changed the tide. Businesspeople providing drones, components and even weapons. Volunteers (including free Russians) joining the Ukrainian military.

This rallying of ordinary people is the crucial leadership message: what wins in the end is driven by our fundamental human sense of justice, which can be seen at the earliest stages of our development as people. These are traits demonstrated in our earliest years. Some children have it beaten out of them through stress (which destroys our capacity for higher thought) and the system.

Most of us retain it, but it can be buried then uncovered by community. In the US around five million people have been turning out for the No Kings protests in a popular rejection of Russell Vought’s plan to turn the US into a Christian Fundamentalist nation along the lines of Saudi Arabia. Supported by the Heritage Foundation (a bunch of rich white sociopaths) and manipulating the intellectually challenged and morally vacuous Mr Trump, they are demonstrating the arrogance of all autocrats - assuming that the sheeple will tolerate them forever. They won’t.

In a vastly less harmful sense, we see this in leadership. The private sector has waged a war on public institutions for many years, mainly through picking away at largely baseless allegations of ‘waste and misuse’ and slow adoption of innovative techniques. But those allegations generally turn out to be wrong.

They feed off the jealousy of stable, full time employment: as a manager in the public service I always thought an important part of my role was to use the opportunity of a well-constructed institution to role-model good employment practice. This sets a benchmark for the private sector, and raises the bar across the board.

Imagine how threatening this is to some employers. The response is to create artificial issues (“I’m just asking the question”)and the attack, driving fear and jealousy implying public employees should exist in a state of fear for their job, because that’s the only way to drive performance.

Utter bullshit. As will be demonstrated when in coming months, Putin will lose, closely followed by Trump, Farage, Seymour and Peters (all of whom are enjoying a resurgence only because the Russian Intelligence Warfare division is supporting them).

The true horror is a the collateral damage that will be caused as they are taken down.

In Aotearoa and the UK it will hopefully be limited to economic damage: Brexit and locally the stone age economics of the National Party and their bizarre attitude to our brand as a nation.

But in the US, Russia and parts of Europe it is in blood.

Business and its leaders must do our part. I see it every day in the (majority of) firms showing that they can think about more than tomorrow, by maintaining a culture and commercial strategy that ignores this short term blip.

They live in the real world. They don’t have problems hiring, because they have a reputation for treating staff well and offering fulfilling work. They are producing things that consumers want, because they aren’t trying to drive growth through enshittification. They are transforming ready for a carbon economy.

We, the people, will win.

item.title: Misplaced Penalties
item.content:encoded:
(Points for getting the connection to the image)

I received an email from school today explaining that the new graduated regime for non-attendance starts this term. It sets out a list of boxes to tick, and what happens if you fail.

As with so many policies copied from the UK, I have been skeptical of the headlines, but hopeful that Aotearoa will take a flawed concept and make it work.

The first thing that struck me was that, as so often, the school appears to have received no communication support. Adult compliance is not something that I expect schools to have a great deal of experience with. Many public sector institutions do not realise that compliance, and Plain English are actually professional areas of expertise and we end up with last minute front line delivery.

This generally takes the form of a letter that fails to convey purpose and approach and (in too many cases) terribly designed forms (if you want to see examples of terrible lawyer-generated forms and communication, have a look at the early work of the Financial Markets Authority).

The Ministry of Education (MinEdu) is a strange beast. Once world leading, years of political interference and populist reckons from ignorant politicians must have made it a soul destroying environment for many. I know that deep in the bowels some excellent research and analysis takes place, but I suspect that the fact everyone thinks they are an expert if they went to school (like everyone who drinks thinks they could run a bar) it is a very trying environment.

The thing that could act as a check on the reckon-based excretions of politicians and talkback hosts might be Our Saviour: Artificial Intelligence.

I turned to AI to see if I could understand the reasoning behind the focus on attendance, and received very thoroughly referenced (which I double checked) responses to questions about the life outcomes of kids who had better attendance, and the best approaches to supporting attendance. TL:DR summary: there is little research showing a direct causal link between persistent, full-time attendance and life outcomes.

When I asked about punitive vs. supportive interventions, the evidence is stark...

...policy guidance and systematic reviews therefore recommend supportive, multi-component interventions (family engagement, case management, attendance supports, early warning systems) rather than punitive parent sanctions.

With this background I would be designing a compliance strategy that led with the actual objective - better life outcomes. That means different things to different people (standardisation is the enemy of innovation).

I’d then have set out the foundations: eliminating barriers to attendance (like being able to afford shoes and transport, and identifying mental health and behavioural issues.)

Only then would I move on to defining a student centred attendance plan that engages parents and caregivers to the extent they are able. Environmental difficulties like taking time off work to attend school meetings, or having to leave for work so you are unable to manage your child out the door in the morning.

I’ve been through all this at a very personal level over the last couple of years, hence having my own reckons.

On looking more closely, NZ policy seems to have leveraged the moronic mutterings of the lesser MPs from ACT and NZF into a reasonable approach based on student engagement. In fact formalising the types of work that dedicated and caring teachers have been doing for many years. Stanford has taken a pigs ear and turned it into a reasonable meal.

So there is plenty of material for a well planned introduction of the ‘new’ policy. It is really just systemising what good teachers and schools have always done. That is a great foundation for a compliance strategy.

If I’d been writing the letter, I wouldn’t have written a letter. But my message would have been:

  • This is how we’ve always approached this. The only real change is how we track it.

  • The government have introduced a structured process so they can measure things.

  • Hopefully that will mean a consistent approach across all schools so it doesn’t matter where you are enrolled. We want to get rid of the post code lottery.

  • We recognise that many barriers to attendance are outside the control of parents.

  • We are here to support you as a family to tackle those.

  • Talk to us and we will try to help.

item.title: Don't call me a realist
item.description: Cynicism, and its even more cowardly sibling, realism, is a beytrayal.
item.content:encoded:
It took me a while to put my finger on it: over the last fortnight I attended the Climate Change Business Conference and the Institute of Directors annual shindig.

The most striking thing that came through was the disconnect between the apparent values of our business leaders in comparison to the politicians who attended (with a couple of exceptions).

It's this: in New Zealand we don't have the legal obligation of shareholder primacy. Under our law the first duty of a Director is to the company, not the shareholders. While it's always front of mind, absolute returns to shareholders are part of the mix, not all of it. We have to consider customers, employees and the broader community within the governance mix.

The language of business is the balance sheet, so of course we need to see that financial outcomes have been considered. Sometimes it is easy - you just can't afford to do, or not do a thing. But those are rarely contentious. The harder part is driving the long term value of the business. What will we be worth in 20 years if we go down this path?

Society creates the economy, not the other way around. Finance is an artificial tool that humans constructed to make it easier to interact for value. It works for us, not us for the economy. That's why it has so much in common with organised religion - money is entirely a matter of faith, and faith depends on trust and belief.

When the economy isn't working for most people, it reaches a point where they lose faith. The foundations of trust in an organised society resides in its institutions, and this is dependent on their integrity, and belief that the rules will be enforced in a fair and transparent way*.

In the noughties, some foreign state actors (FSA’s - Russia and Iran being the leaders, North Korea & China learning quickly) were handed a new tool with which to weaken their state rivals in The West: democratic countries that maintain the rule of law. Social media gave a vector to achieve a marketers dream - individually targeted messaging that was propagated though a high-trust connection. The most effective misinformation is delivered by friends and relatives.

This landed with an audience that did not have the tools to differentiate between lies shared by a high-trust source (say, a family member) and truths shared by someone with which we have no personal connection. In the intelligence world, we rate source and content separately. When people are looking at the shitstream on InstaDick or TwatTock, not so much. This was especially true of early adopters on that tool of the elderly, FalseBook. Russia’s modus operandi is to seed false stories and ‘research’ on puppet outlets in the west, start the propagation and then deny them. They pay the puppets to take any flak.

There followed a steady and conscious development of information warfare tradecraft that allowed FSA's to target democracies at their weakest point at a lower cost and with a geographic isolation never seen before in our history. Pamphleteers and papers required physical connection. The Internet doesn't. And the very tool itself could be used to minimise the outcomes of detection.

Business leaders were relatively early adopters of this new mechanism. They largely approached it like any other, and I wonder if it meant many quickly learned how easy it is to manipulate people, giving themselves some protection from the bullshit?

Politicians seized on the new tools. The US is, as so often, led the way. Mr Obama was an early adopter: his team saw the opportunity and took it, reaching out in a very targeted way to electors. But so did the New (post-Nixon) Republican party. You can't beat demographics, and social / Christian conservatives knew that they would eventually go the way of their boomer base. So they started taking over the party, using the god of monetarism (a bullshit theory initiated by Milton Friedman) as their gospel. In the UK it was called Thatcherism. It denied that there is any value in society. Money was the only credible decision factor. It's still alive and well in a certain demographic.

In business we know that is not true. It sets constraints, but there is no specific time frame over which it should be considered. Long term value comes from the Golden Goose, not the eggs that it lays. Business has more interest in nurturing a sustainable ongoing market: customers who want and can afford to buy the product, an environment that is not riven by climate change and happy, engaged and productive employees who keep it all going.

Contrast this with powerful but cynical subset of politicians, manipulated by a group of political consultants who will never see an income directly from government (more puppets). That's a key point: if you support a politician into power (and you are not independently wealthy) what do you gain from the effort? We tend to focus on lobbying, but in reality it is far more complex. Why does the Atlas Network (funded largely by gun manufacturers) support ACT? Why did the Russian-linked "Bad Boys of Brexit" arrive to help NZFirst with their political campaign? Why did Russia target New Zealand so heavily in 2020? And how does it affect credibility when misinformation is supplied to you by a source you trust?

As Directors, we mostly require more than my nanna sent me this to justify a business case. Most people don't have that type of guardrail. So perhaps we have been a bit more protected from the shitstream?

The overwhelming impression I got from both conferences is that, while tolerating a political landscape where minor parties rely on fear and divisiveness for support, business leaders are pretty underwhelmed by politicians of the centre who are meant to stand up to the extremes. There was not a groundswell of support when junior ministers or even the Prime Minister walked in - it was much more at the eye rolling end of the spectrum.

What was very obvious is that business sees the benefits of diversity (culture, age, gender, race) and facing up to the universal challenge of climate change. There's no business case to pushing and ideological argument based on lies and demonisation. Our job is to accept reality and work with it, not hark back to a fantasy world when it was always summertime and the living was easy.

I found it uplifting, and it reminded me I shouldn't be frightened of getting out among my peers: I must embrace it. Most leaders are thoughtful, decent people who want to make the world better. It’s when we get conned into the destructive cycle of fear, hate and cynicism that it all goes wrong. And I didn’t hear once the phrase “I’m just a realist”. Maybe more people are coming to my view that realist means coward.

item.title: Climate Change Business Conference 2025
item.content:encoded:
September 9, 2025

A message that came through clearly at the #CCBC25 is the (hopefully temporary) handbrake that has been put on New Zealand Climate Change leadership. Ambassadors from China and Europe were able to highlight their leadership position: MFAT came across as disappointingly constrained.

We know that we currently have two parties in parliament that clearly live in a parallel universe that was created and supported by a state actor utterly dependent on oil revenue to sustain an insane, domestically driven war. They are joined by the usual suspects - a fossil industry that has so much money available that their influence can only be tackled by governments.

We are being left behind. We punched above our weight, almost entirely to (let's be honest) a questionable track record of being clean and green.

We know that the election of politicians with fossilised views (those hanging on to ideas that were complete cobblers the day they were written down and haven't improved with time, such as neoliberalism) was driven by three things from a cohort of angry voters wedded to a strange, overly simplistic worldview driven by fear ("if you see something, say something"), envy ("I've worked hard for what I have, but others are doing better because of all those bludgers") and health issues (dementia symptoms arising from age, social media and long term Covid impact).

The major parties aren't supplying much in the way of leadership or answers. They hired political strategists over the last few years who are obsessed with social media. They are told the reckons of the deranged on social media are representative. They are not. But when you are hammer everything looks like a nail. This leaves a gulf between the 'professional' advice our political leaders receive and what voters are really seeking.

And that is why the major parties are lost. They can't reconcile the fact as individual MP's they sacrifice their personal beliefs on the alter of strategic marketing while failing to build their base. The process of becoming a candidate is horrendous - intelligence officers are probably subject to fewer attacks on their ego than someone who wants to stand for National.

That beats the fight out them. By the time they are in the house they have been surrounded by so many cynical apparatchiks for so long they struggle to lead, to take something they feel passionately about and see it through.

The small parties find things much easier. They don't rely on professionals as much. Their objective is easier to attain - they don't need many voters. They will happily suborn themselves to ridiculous commitments (reducing tobacco regulation, enabling fossil fuel exploration) in return for modest funding. Because they only need to market to a small group of fossilised minds.

That gives us hope. Those who are least rational tend to be male and / or old. That means they will not be voting much longer. If we follow the UK and lower the voting age we get further help. Young males have less well developed higher thought functions - we didn't evolve to plan ahead much, so simply don't have the imagination to think strategically compared to women at that age. On the plus side males seem more likely to go down the why bother to vote path.

The voters of the last 30+ years have utterly failed the planet, and their species. They have shown themselves to be gullible, cynical and self interested. They love their children, but don't care about our children (or we'd have a universal basic income for kids as well as pensioners). And we have lost the chance to limit global warming to 1.5C.

We still can manage an overshoot and a return to 1.5C, but the longer we leave it the harder it will be. That won't happen unless we turn against the (very) wealthy who appear to have decided that their money will save them from 8 billion starving people. In fact, I have a sneaking suspicion they think they will live forever (hint: when people are hungry, the pig you grew for spare organs isn't going to last long enough to harvest them.)

Real, productive business in New Zealand is ignoring the politicians. Their obligation is to the business, it's customers and a sustainable future. They are not beholden to a small group of noisy opinionated voters who are more worried about trans rights and vaccine myths than whether their grandchildren will be caught up in the chaos of a chaotic and dangerous future climate.

This was reinforced for me at #CCBC25 while watching 5 MP's on stage from the leading parties. National, Act and NZF were embarrassing, undignified and really had no substantive message. They were in denial about the realities of life ("they're going to flood half the course where I play golf") and wedded to the past. The brightest point was Swarbrick, who offered an alternative vision. When she pressed the others hard, they simply responded with deflection and name calling. Because they have no answers. It was acutely cringeworthy if the Ambassadors from the EU and China were still in the audience.

Businesses are not wasting their time with facile, fantasy arguments from mainstream parties: they are dealing every day with the real demands of society and their customers. They are tackling the challenges today that arise from climate change: market access, customer sentiment, investment mandates, fossil fuel price uncertainty.

Our part as citizens is to stop judging politicians on what they say, but what they do. Pay attention. Get your priorities right and get out and vote in a way that doesn't reward foreign tech bro's for creating chaos.

item.title: Freedom or Crucifixion?
item.content:encoded:
Around the world people are sensing that the failed economic policies of the last forty years or so are close to crumbling. Some wait with baited breath for a political movement to emerge that has the courage to show a path forward. Others are keen to accelerate the destruction of the western hegemony, ranging from smart state actors (Mr. Putin) to the ignorant and deranged (Mr. Trump).

And then there are a significant number of people, mainly Baby Boomers and Gen's X & Y who bought into the dream, and can't quite let it go. They know something went wrong: they did what they were told. They saved (many seeing that money disappear in fees and failures). They think they worked hard. They accepted the need to retrain into new jobs. They took the redundancy from their skilled work and moved to service industries. Their houses are worth a fortune, but still they struggle. None of it worked for them.

They feel betrayed.

I'm not going to labour the reasons why monetarism is fundamentally flawed: it simply fails to grasp that the economy is a social construct that exists because of society. People create the system in which the economy exists, not the other way around. Plenty of smarter people than me have explained this in detail.

But I can give a couple of examples of examples how politicians and senior public servants get things wrong in the New Zealand context. And the more conservative, sociopathic ("realists") or populist the party, the harder they seem to find it to let go of history.

Hypothesis #1: small economies should not try to copy big economies. It needs to play to its strengths, change the basis of competition. Here in Aotearoa we have a frustrating tendency to copy our colonial not-so-superpower (for public policy), or look to the USA as an example of how the private sector should operate. We will never out-British the UK, and we will never out American the USA. So why do we look to them as leaders? Why do we not look to the type of society we'd like to become for our role model?

Westminster is one of the most bureaucratic, flawed, over engineered public services in the world. When I am working in post colonial countries I sometime wonder if it was a deliberate strategy to cripple colonies as the British left. Following Brexit, people seem to be (finally) discovering that perhaps it was the UK that drove the red tape, not the EU. The UK ranks 8th for ease of doing business - New Zealand is #1. And that doesn't count ease of living. As an example, have a look at the regulations (and costs) involved in owning and using a car.

The United States ranks 6th for ease of doing business. As anyone who has set up an operation there will tell you, the administration is like stepping back in time. No nice universal Companies Act to set the basic rules. Rafts of State and local tax and compliance burdens. Systems that range from exceptional to Victorian. And they still use cheques. But perhaps most off-putting, in a system where the State leaves most commercial law to be self policed (i.e. businesses sue each other. A lot.) there is nothing to balance relative power. Might becomes right: big business can simply out-spend the little guy. In New Zealand it is the Act party who seem to believe that private contracts and absolute property rights are more important than society.

Hypothesis #2: we rely on truthiness and oversimplified arithmetic to justify decisions. One example is the idea that big is more efficient, also known as economies of scale. It is true that big things often do better than small, but this may have nothing to do with efficiency: often it is about power balance. We've probably all bumped into the economy of scale graph. But how often do you see the whole picture? It looks like this, showing that sometimes bigger means more expensive. We should be aiming for SRAC2 or 3, not 4 or 5.

I'm a fan of Porters 5 Forces, a simple way of thinking about using power for competitive advantage. Next time you see a strategic move ostensibly based on economy of scale, think about it in terms of market influence. It can be revealing. And I suspect it is why so many mergers fail.

But back to the main point: for over forty years we have watched economic theory and the pseudo-maths that backs it used to bamboozle, baffle and bullshit us into thinking that neoliberalism was rational. It isn't. The arithmetic adds up, but that doesn't mean the underlying assumption is valid. Individuals value being safe and fed far above other life goals. And for working people it's hard to have enough time and wisdom to make perfect personal decisions at all times.

The purpose of the theory was to provide an intellectual vehicle to enable a (relatively) small class of people to self-justify a power grab. And it worked, reversing a long term improvement in the Gini coefficient (a measure of the difference in wealth between the rich and the poor.) What monetarism basically does is disconnect money from social value. That's why this government hates the concept of wellbeing. They don't want you to be well. They want you to sell yourself into economic servitude by loading up with debt.

We should be grateful to Heritage (and to some extent Atlas) for their honesty. Project 2025 was a manifesto for turning back political structures by around 200 years, to the time when you only got to vote if you were male and had money. They carry on a long tradition in the US that has its roots in the civil war, but manifested strongly since the 1950's as a response to the growing consensus that, having seen the horrors of fascism, many troops came home wanting something better for their children. There was broad support in the West for strong social support mechanisms, not only because it is right, but also as a barrier to the re-emergence of Nazi's.

Those troops had seen first hand how populism turned otherwise decent men into barbarians by stoking a fear of 'others'. Because others provide a useful scapegoat to distract from the real causes of societal problems.

The trigger for the takeover came around 1973. That was the last time Republicans went up to a President and said “if you don’t resign, we will impeach you’. And he did. The Republican party was then taken over, and eventually a core group worked in the US and UK to promote a new type of economics. The Reagan / Thatcher axis was formed. (New Zealand, having been cut off from the UK by the Common Market, grasped around for a way to cope, and eventually followed a similar path).

It was crucial to the new Republican party that those likely to vote Democrat were disenfranchised, and while it was Southern Democrats who were once famous for gaming electoral maps, the worst offenders for the last 40 years or so have been Republican States. In the UK Thatcher took a different approach, introducing the Poll Tax ("Community Charge"), so nicknamed because the only way to avoid the tax was to give up voting: it was a tax based on membership of the electoral roll.

Rolling the clock forward we face a perfect storm. A wealthy elite utterly disconnected from society. The middle classes under pressure from rising costs and reducing opportunities. An existential crisis from Climate Change. The creation of a right wing (prosperity gospel) church that bears little resemblance to the teachings of Christ, but justifies abhorrent behaviour. A kleptocrat waging war in Europe for no obvious reason, and blatantly promoting unrest through information warfare. And widespread use of technology platforms that magnify the unhinged like never before. Fascism emerging across the US, Russia and Israel, emboldening constraints on liberty even in benign countries.

History shows this tends to head down one of two paths.

A new, moderate reformist movement emerges. Using relatively benign methods within the bounds of the rule of law, wealth is redistributed, abuses are curtailed and key enablers (media oligopolies and monopolies) tackled. This happened in the US following the Great Depression. The New Deal led to an unbroken streak of prosperity that lasted 50 years or so (depending on how you count it). You only have to look at the attacks on Zohran Mamdani to realise how frightened the conservative movement is of this option.

Alternatively, frustration builds, populism is exploited. There is often a hiccup when the leadership comes to fear the power of their supporters, and there is a purge to consolidate power. But that is just a sign of it doubling down. Eventually civilisation returns, but with a great deal of collateral damage on the way through, including of the leadership.

Who will be our saviour? That’s a tough one, because the backdrop of vitriol makes the barrier to entering politics very high. Who would want to stand and be on the receiving end of the unhinged outpourings of a bunch of angry (lets face it) men? Who would want to face the stream of made-up outrage that drives the business model of a nonagenarian Australian?

Perhaps the answer is to hope for King Arthur to return after all.

item.title: The Power of Outrage
item.content:encoded:
The Christchurch massacre was a defining moment in the history of NZ. A biblical “we shall hunt them down blah blah” would have been a typical response. And the outcome would have been escalation, further feeding the insanity of the right wing element in our society.

Instead, Prime Minister Ardern chose another path. And that was the reason that, passing through Dubai soon after, I was met with her picture on the worlds tallest building.

The legacy of this particular PM is sullied by the massive inferiority complex that dogs a small but vocal minority of NZ. It’s easier to say a woman or special interest group has received an unfair advantage than acknowledge that maybe your ego is bigger than your capability.

Onto that fertile ground of the dispossessed, those who believed in Thatcher and Reagan and Friedman and did what they were told, only to find forty years later their life was even harder… in that parched soil appeared the seeds of conflict. Among those for whom fear and anger are a market opportunity there arose potential for growth. Frightened people buy guns and mistrust authority. When different races and classes fight with one another, they lose sight of who really causes the problems (hint: they generally wear a collar and tie.)

But a threat had arisen. What if that one event, a compassionate white woman showing care and love for her brothers and sisters ... started a movement? What if ordinary people stopped being angry with the anonymous and started seeing people, with all the same hopes and fears? What if enemy became… humanized?

And so the Prime Minister of a tiny country in the backwaters of the Pacific got on the radar. It isn’t some great conspiracy. There’s no bunker with a whiteboard1 mapping out some sort of demonic plan for global domination. There are just some political consultants, pollsters and pawns, and some naive old men who will do anything to be in the spotlight.

Except when a State Actor becomes involved. Then a whole new set of capabilities are brought to the table.

It is the beauty of this approach is that there is no conspiracy. There is no big plan. Because the only thing required is to stoke the fires of outrage. Keep the hatred smouldering. You don’t need specific outcomes. You just need to make sure people become cynical about their leaders. Mistrustful. Victims within their own society.

You will have met them: they are the people who repeat salacious bullshit. They will be disproportionately bent out of shape about trans-rights, gay marriage and other things that probably don’t affect them. They will protest they are being silenced, that free speech is an absolute right. They will speak in a manner that presents their achievements as brilliance and their failures as bad luck (when in reality it is probably the other way around). And the definitive diagnostic: “I’m just asking the question”.

These people have been manipulated. They may be at higher risk of dementia, Alzheimers or Parkinson’s. They may have been someone you respected, who now seems to burble undignified piffle. Do not think that presenting a coherent counter-argument using your ruthless logic will change their minds. They think they arrived at this place themselves, and to unpick that could cause severe psychological damage. Back off. The response to a victim is compassion, not anger. Because a retort simply feeds the internet-enabled outrage-machine that is at the root of the problem.

If they were conscious of how they are being manipulated then I would call them traitors. Too many of them present wilful blindness as an excuse. Stark examples are Brexit, and Russian interference in the 2016 US election campaign, so thoroughly investigated and proven by the (Republican-led) investigation. Mr Putins goals for Project Lakhta are clearly set out, and (credit where it is due) highly successful:

  1. Increase political and social discord within the United States

  2. Sabotage the Clinton campaign

  3. Support the election of Trump

The Internet Research Agency (a Russian troll farm) was employed to use any opportunity to criticise Hillary Clinton and the rest of the candidates. If you know people who repeat the key fallacies promoted by these methods (crooked Hillary etc.) then they are victims of the plan. Be gentle with them, they have been psychologically abused.

This is asymmetric warfare, because the objectives of either side are vastly different. Developed, democratic nations want stability, the rule of law, human rights and an economy that offers equal opportunities for development.

The state actors simply want instability. The Russian economy (especially today) shows no hope of catching up with the US. China is a different story. But if you can’t drive innovation and growth, the next best thing is to hinder the opposition. The US economy will crater over the coming yearss due to the Kwasicide of the orange toddlers economic policies, and it will take years to recover. That’s a win.

We must acknowledge that imperial powers, first the British and then the US have brought this upon themselves through a long history of abuse of weaker countries. We as the collective West need to own that.

We can fight this threat, and the way is simple. Relentless compassion and kindness. Putting right our past mistakes. It works.

And where our politicians won’t stand up, business leaders must.

Mr Putin prefers glass and grease marker. They don’t dry out.

item.title: Cognitive Dissonance
item.description: March 2025: the dangers of truthiness in economics
item.content:encoded:
In 2016, the United Kingdom (supported by Putins outrage machine), voted to separate from its largest trading partner. The process took a while, but actually happened in 2020. In the years since it turns out that pretty much every economic prediction made by those who wanted to remain turned out to be correct. There are about 2 million fewer jobs in Britain now than had they remained in the EU. GDP is 4% lower, and well over one Trillion pounds of assets have moved off-shore. Euronext has replaced the London Stock Exchange as largest in Europe. EU buyers of property have been replaced largely by the Chinese, but real property prices have fallen. Oh, and immigration to the UK is how at its highest level. Ever.

In a desperate move, Prime Minister Liz Truss (6 Sep - 25 Oct 2022. That’s not a typo.) pushed an extreme budget through parliament. Central to it was the theory (reminiscent of a piece of bullshitonomics called the Laffer curve) that drastic tax cuts would promote growth. It further cratered the British economy. 40% of mortgage products were withdrawn due to the likelihood of rapid base-rate rises. Government borrowing costs rose sharply. Sterling collapsed.

The US is in the process of rolling out all the same mistakes, based on the same failed ideologies, supported by the Atlas Network and The Heritage Foundation. It will cripple many of the businesses that provide the foundation of Americas prosperity. Inflation will surge. Borrowing costs and public debt will balloon. Unemployment will spike. It will hasten the demise of the US dollar as the global reserve currency.

And, as with Brexit (again, strongly supported by a gleeful Russia) this will happen while ordinary people, the ones who will pay the price, are distracted by that age old trope: a fear of others.

Update: in January 2025 I moved my retirement savings into a conservative (bond weighted) fund. Everything in Trumps project plan (aka Project 2025) signalled economic disaster.

I then watched as share markets excitedly pumped themselves up on good metrics emerging from the Trump economy.

Increasing though the markets became concerned that many of the statistics they relied on seemed to be bullshit. And in July the shoe dropped: turns out the numbers were wrong. The US economy is in trouble.

And there’s a reason for that. The Trump government didn’t just gut foreign and public broadcasting: they crippled the bureau of statistics.

The story of an amazing American economy is just another steaming pile of bullshit.

item.title: The Emperor's New Clothes

Payrolls increased 73,000 in July after the prior two months were revised down by nearly 260,000, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics report out Friday. In the last three months, employment growth has averaged a paltry 35,000 — the worst since the pandemic.**

item.title: "It has been said that history repeats itself. This is perhaps not quite correct; it merely rhymes."
item.content:encoded:
Often attributed to Mark Twain, this is a quote from Theodor Reik's 1965 essay “The Unreachables”.

If, like me, you are watching the unfolding madness in the US and wondering WTF is going on, look no further that Germany in the 1930's.

Conservatism is, by definition, applied to groups that have a vested interest in the status quo. There is a crucial business and governance aspect to this. Conservative groups have built a capital asset that they wish to protect whether it be a military industrial complex or a societal norm that favours their position. They are genuinely so arrogant they believe us plebs know no better.

Demographics drive our economy. Not so long ago conservative elements saw the writing on the wall (they can afford the best analysis) and realised that their future was doomed. In an economy based on services, capital assets lose their power. If you own oil assets, your power is lost in a renewable economy.

They started planning for a future where democracy would no longer work for them. And so organisations like the Atlas and Heritage Foundations were co-opted by money. They are echoes, or rhymes, of the feudal lords of old who wanted to maintain the status quo to retain their power. The irony of the 'no Kings' protests.

The opposite of capitalism is not socialism. It is progression. It is people who want a liberalism that threatens conservatives. Unfortunately the term liberal has been co-opted (in NZ it is the ACT party who control the term 'liberal')

Fascism inevitably turns to conservatism for its power. If you would like to see a rhyming playbook for what is happening in the USA today, we have one.

In the last few months Trump has, guided by the Project 2025 movement, replaced the General Staff of the US military and the senior staff of the Judge Advocate Generals office: the people who decide whether the US military are following 'lawful orders'. I am heartened by the resistance shown by the US military. Trump is not their heritage, and I am confident they will prevail. Eventually.

item.title: WFH in the Big Leather Chair
item.description: Published March 24, 2020 at the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic.
item.content:encoded:
It turned out that a lot of large organisations made a fuss about their remote working policies... Immigration NZ were so bad they basically stopped work (leading to a massive backlog).

My firm (TICC) moved everyone home a couple of weeks prior to lockdown, found project work while looking for other income streams, were already on an allowance based system and had the security & safety approach finalised. We had the advantage of a no-committee environment.

The picture of Churchill references a man who slapped the British bureaucracy around when they failed to grasp that in an emergency sometimes the rules don’t matter any more.

We're all getting used to being at home - it's that BCP many created but somehow never really thought they'd use in anger, the eyes rolling at the word 'pandemic' on the risk register...

So having been employed from home for much of this millenium, I thought I'd share a few thoughts for setting up your home workers especially in the context of handling sensitive information.

I'm not going to go link crazy in here: this is when leaders need to step up, and I am not using any terms or brand names that shouldn't be familiar to a competent leader in the twenty first century. That's why you get the big leather chair.

The basics: I can't do better than CERTNZ. This should be your go-to source of guidance. I especially like their password advice which is way ahead of most private sector brand names and financial institutions.

The Asset: many telecommuting (remember that phrase?) policies are obsessed with trivia - they are more worried about the value of the physical device than the information access portal it represents. Tell your accountants to get back in their box - this is not their time. A Chromebox with a really good screen will cost you less than NZ$1,000 - the cost of the machine isn't the problem, except for the difficulty of replacing it if it gets nicked.

Internet Trauma: the next legacy hangover are policies that are terrified a delicate soul may see a rude word on the internet. Long gone are the days when anyone gave a shit (sic) about minor offence, so don't get buried in Victorian concerns about what your staff may look at in a browser on your machine. There is only so much you can do, and the world knows this.

OK, so here are a few ideas that might be more useful than the computer use policy published in 2002:

If you don't pay a data and device allowance, sort it out. The easiest way to make ownership of a suitable smartphone with a data allowance a condition of employment is to pay for it. $35 a month is 50% of a 30Gb 4G plan with unlimited calls and texts. Easy. That means you can then mandate all sorts of productivity tools like rostering, Trello for work planning and so on - all the stuff that we use in the modern era to make work more effective. This hasn't had an FBT issue for donkeys years, so don't get distracted by accountants blithering (see paragraph near the end).

Physical Safety & Security is often overlooked: If conceivably possible, do a site inspection (by Whatsapp on their phone - see above). This allows you to check for a number of real risks. Is their internet fast enough (SpeedTest app)? Have the default credentials on their WiFi been changed (ask / photo of router), and is it password protected?

More importantly, do they have an ergonomically safe workstation? Look at the ACC and Worksafe sites to find out what this means. Can they work it a location where people can't see over their shoulder?

Each morning, issue a code word by email and ask your home workers to reply attaching a photo of the machine in situ with that code word in plain sight on the screen. This confirms nothing significant has changed from the set up that you agreed.

Verify the machine settings: your geek will do this, but if you are lucky you won't need to connect to a legacy directory service (another advantage of GSuite etc.). The machine should have locked down local administration rights and an encrypted drive - this is Secuity 101 stuff, so don't get tricked into thinking it's a big job: it's starting to sound like rocket science, change your IT advisor, quickly. Remote management comes built in to most systems nowadays but make sure it is working. Skype will do the trick.

Work in the cloud. Some people still whine about this, especially those who think MS Outlook with an amazing folder structure is a good thing. Now isn't the moment to fix their thinking completely, but if you are lucky you are in GSuite or Office 365 already. If so, use it in a browser (Chrome or Safari). It mitigates so many security risks.

No printers. Just stop it. Printer = ink, paper and a decent shredder. If you have someone insisting their eyes can't cope, and don't have a really solid letter from a specialist to that effect, then read the next paragraph carefully. Personally I actually find it quite insulting to people who have genuine medical grounds.

If people don't need to work, then don't make them. There can be a sense that if you are paying someone, they should do something. But actually this is the moment when your Sergeants should be at the fore. You will likely have a whole strata of middle managers and administrators who will only confuse things - remember, this is survival mode. Don't be afraid to let the overheads coast. Maybe give them a project, perhaps that planning exercise with the word Enterprise or Transformation in the description that has been on the to-do list. But make sure you keep them out of the way of the people who actually generate business value during this crucial time. It is quite possible the best option from a security and efficiency point of view is to gently grant special leave. I can think of dozens of people I have encountered in my working life in this category, so don't be afraid, and don't think it signals past failures of your leadership.

Make sure your preferred chat system is working and that people feel free to use it. Dip in so people know you are there, but don't use it as a platform for your ego. Pay attention and genuinely respond if you see the right moment. But don't schedule a regular update - patterns signal pandering, and they end up feeling forced. People can tell when your Board has told the CEO to send out something: it isn't in the right voice.

Above all, this is a time to be kind, not remind people of policies and rules. This is your moment to quietly kill the bullshit, and just be part of a community trying to look after each other.

item.title: Devaluing our Identity
item.content:encoded:
This is an East German identity card. I suspect the USA is currently working out how to connect their myriad ‘Government ID’ credentials to background information checks so when the time comes undesirables can be identified. Think I’m paranoid? 1 2 3

If history does indeed rhyme, one of the regular beats is a call for a centralised identity system to make it easier to do stuff. But the flip side of identity validation is identity theft - in a system reliant on a single ID token, the prize for a villain gaining a false authentication is much higher.

In 2016 New Zealand rolled out phase II of its programme for countering money laundering, creating another tranche of reporting entities storing copies of identity documents, usually in the same place as they keep home address, date of birth, tax file numbers and possibly bank account details. Ironically the only thing they probably won't store are credit card numbers, because the Payment Card Industry realised how dangerous this was and have put in place standards far higher than many governments (amazing how motivational financial loss can be).

When I talk to firms that need to manage identity information I emphasise that they have specific statutory obligations to store such records in a secure manner and destroy them once they are no longer needed. They have been granted legal authority as an agent of the State to request them, but it is disappointing that the guidance given by Government tends to ficus the validation with little attention paid to making sure that the duty of care for your personal information is understood.

It would be nice to see, say, the Privacy Commissioner funded to carry out a campaign targeting reporting entities (including an independent audit programme) to ensure all those copies of your passport are being looked after.

And there is another effect that is eroding the security of your identity: this legitimate proliferation of demand for identity documents is normalising the behaviour. We should be clear: ID documents don’t do much to deter crime, but they can help after-the-fact. Making it normal to demand a high-value identity document for trivial reasons not only increases the level of fear in society, it increases the risk of identity related crime through proliferation of documents.

One of the craziest I’ve seen recently was a firm called XPO Exhibitions who demand that you send them a copy of your drivers licence, passport or photo credit card before they will allow you into a craft exhibition. I’m sure this meets some important business objective to do with the terrible risk of hordes of civilians wanting to look at greeting cards, but it doesn’t take into account the potential cost to their customers; they have clearly not stopped to consider the risks.

And perhaps more importantly the only legal breaches (I can think of three possibilities) are weak and un-policed. I don't want to pick on these guys, but they are representative of an increasing trend that will serve to weaken legitimate requirements over time.

With mandatory notification has helped: in 2017 if XPO’s filing cabinet / mail server full of your identity documents was to be stolen they would have the option of keeping quiet . Chances are nobody will ever figure out where that spate of identity theft originated. But now they would likely have to report this, allowing protective action (and hopefully the chance to sue: did I mention that financial risk tends to be a good motivator?).

But we must all take responsibility for looking after our identity. Don’t casually allow people to copy your documents - it is usually just an illusion of security anyway. When the library asks to copy your drivers licence to take out a book when you’ve left your library card at home (that really happened to me), challenge it (they backed down).

The crazy thing is that showing them your LinkedIn profile is arguably a better form of ID anyway.

item.title: Extinction or Transformation
item.description: Updated from a post first published August 10, 2022
item.content:encoded:
In the Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy, a wholly remarkable book (and all you need to understand modern life) is a short section about the parable of the reason. Adams tells a story about how a messenger travels bewteen two warring peoples. By the time he gets to the destination, he forgets why the argument that seemed so reasonable when he set out now makes no sense.

It’s reminiscent of those encounters we have with the dinosaurs of our economy, banks, financial services and utilities. Listening to their odd language and logic, you can sometimes leave the room wondering how you’ve managed to survive so long.

For surely the only organisations less competent than internet provider call centres must be the banks.

As I get older I am delighted that I rarely have to deal with the moronic parallel universe that is the banking sector. If someone had explained to me that one of the only constants throughout my life would be the inanity of banks and university admission processes I wouldn't have believed them. But here I am.

I do a bit of advisory for businesses looking for capital, and probably the most challenging aspects are the rare occasions dealing with the mainstream banks. It’s like stepping into the land that time forgot from a process perspective, and for someone who knows quite a lot about AML and onboarding the breathtaking incompetency only makes me hope they are better at making sure my ledger balances (to be fair, they are - the team shovelling coal into the mainframes in the basement are the most competent part of the operation).

Reserve banks and tax authorities globally (including our own) have been very slowly bringing pressure to bear on the asset base of the banking sector. This has been crucial to counteract the flawed monetary response to 2008 (which our disappointingly staid government went along with at the time: "let's leave that for someone else to deal with"). Luckily it was a one off disaster. Imagine if we’d had earthquakes, pandemic, war and shocks to the global economy since then?

You can’t beat mean reversion and demographics, and in our faith-based monetary system the latter has a huge effect. Older people are less profitable. Margin pressure must eventually increase.

Banks make their money by borrowing (off us) and lending (to us) a bit higher. Older people tend to simply put their money on term deposit. As there are fewer of them, access to this cheap source of capital reduces. As the ratio between income and house prices resets (especially in countries reducing immigration) then the other big asset the banks keep on their books (your house) loses its relative value.

There’s a good explanation of how this works here:

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/561626/where-does-money-come-from-are-home-loans-actually-fake

If mainstream banks have to shift their focus, it’s going to be a shock to the system. AI may not be optimal (as picking winning business models involves understanding emotion). Selling mortgages is easy, so the management tier of banks can understand it. Lending to business is not, requiring knowledge, wisdom, life experience and judgement.

The banks have forgotten how to do small to medium business. Basically it was cheaper to shift the risk to an asset (i.e. make the business person secure the debt against their house) than pay for staff who could understand how a business in the real economy works.

I’ve dealt with all five of the main banks over the last few years. On the rare occasion I’ve encountered someone good they don’t last long. The culture seems to grind them down. Banks tend to recruit from one another, so it becomes a self-fulfilling cycle of mediocrity. It is telling that ex-bankers tend to struggle if they leave to work in the productive sector.

Under this attack the sector appears to have adopted a defensive posture, retreating further into comfortable mediocrity. The share market illustrates how they are regarded by professional investors. bank shares are a commodity, the market churns them according to portfolio rules and the news cycle. None of the individual banks show any particular competitive advantage, the only skill required is how to leverage the value of the money-printing license. Only fools take a strategic long term stake in a specific bank, far easier to buy the sector.

But perhaps most damning is that on our side of the world (unlike, say, Germany) the sector is not part of our competitive advantage as a nation. This is a sector that caused the global financial crisis... then made money when 'we the people' printed money to bail them out. This is a sector that couldn't even manage to lend government backed money. This is a sector that actively sabotages government support efforts, by treating soft government loans as substitute for their lending (rather than allowing it to be used for growth as intended.)

It's time we took a good hard look at the sector and asked what we as a society want from it in return for the licence we grant. Is it too much to ask that it supports business growth? Is it right that we have to task government agencies with supporting businesses because the banks won't?

I'd like to see a Royal Commission, but with different terms to Australia (which was about culture.) It needs to focus on what role we want banks to play. For example, one approach would be to re-establish the State Advances Act (which was only repealed in 2019) and provide a simple government home savings and loan scheme. This worked well for decades, and perhaps it is not a coincidence that banking profits from the sector took off when the government support was removed. It should also look at practices such as mandating the use of specific law firms (so the purchasing decision is removed from those who actually pay the bill - what could possibly go wrong?)

But we have to do something. We have a productivity problem, and part of that is due to poor levels of capital investment to drive efficiency. And now is the time - we are going to have to fund an economic transformation on a larger scale than post war reconstruction. The banks need to get on board or get out of the way.
