https://thegreatdepressionofthe30s.weebly.com/significant-impact.html

I’m not sure what is more frustrating: politicians on the right still promoting long discredited economic truthiness, or watching them try and hide it behind the tired old tax cuts argument. I had hoped watching Truss and Kwarteng destroying years of economic growth overnight would perhaps have knocked it for six, but locally our right of centre party (National) are still trotting out deeply flawed economic fantasies, perhaps playing on the Republicans games in Congress.

Both use the same argument: tax cuts will drive economic growth, compensating for the short term pain of inflation. Despite the fact that tax cuts are inflationary.

We find ourselves in a situation that has some parallels with the lead up to the Great Depression. Inflation, wealth disparity and over-inflated asset prices (which collapsed, hurting a lot of people.) At the time, economic theory was about balancing the books, treating national accounts like running a household (or company) budget. The result was a feedback loop that destroyed businesses and lives.

The disaster eventually led to some of our greatest social and economic achievements: social security, universal healthcare, state housing, education reform and Keynesian economics.

The latter was displaced by monetary theory (the foundation of what is often termed neo-liberal economics) in the eighties. It has failed.

The root of the problem is an extreme form of money illusion. This is when people forget that money isn’t an end in itself, merely a means to an end. Beautiful minds forgot that the economy is an expression of society, not a state of nature. Economics is a branch of anthropology, not mathematics. They got cause and effect muddled up, confusing correlation with causation.

The "cost of living crisis" is caused by a divergence of income from asset values. The answer is redistribution. We need to reduce the real value of assets, and convert them into income. In practical terms that means wage and benefit rises for the lower income brackets.

This does not mean tax cuts. Moving bands and changing the rates for lower brackets disproportionately benefits the wealthy. Move all the bands up and the people who benefit most are those on higher incomes. And the problem is they then bid more for assets, driving up prices, because they don’t need to fritter the extra income away on things like food and clothes for their children. In a nation with low productivity growth, that means inflation.

Most successful countries have measures to apply economic friction to asset values - they tax those gains. New Zealand does not. This in adds a multiplier effect to anything that benefits higher income earners, and we’re back to a destructive feedback loop.

Democracies depend on a strong opposition. It is disappointing to hear tired and disproven theories trotted out to please a party base. The cynic in me thinks it is simply to assist in election fundraising from (wealthy) donors. The price is long term damage to the economy, and more importantly our social structure.

Unless you have Victorian ears, I would recommend this explanation of the economic issues at play from that great educational institution, The Juice Media. Warning: this video contains strong language, just like real life.

https://www.thejuicemedia.com/honest-government-ad-reserve-bank-of-australia/

item.title: A Crisis of Competence
item.content:encoded:
Me and the team at IRD, c2004 https://www.facebook.com/nostalgickiwi/videos/1981-gliding-on-intro/1373522846029166/

The question of effectiveness and efficiency has been troubling me recently, probably because I am in one of those periods of dealing with various government agencies and banks.

But it has a lot of relevance to the current election campaign which is turning out to be one of the most depressingly ignorant and cynical that I can remember. There are a bunch of vocal nutters good for a headline of course, and politicians who are happy to lend a hook for them to hang their bigotry on. ("Let's take back our country". From whom, precisely, Winston?)

So why do so many bureaucracies seem to be determined to reinforce a popular view that the basic processes by which our life is managed are broken? Why is it so many people in banks and government departments seem to have given up? After many years of failed attempts at over-automation, why do customer facing organisations still persist with pushing their processes to their customers, rather than owning the opportunity?

It's not that the people who do the work want to be de-skilled: survey after survey shows that most employees want to be trained and given the opportunity to make their job more interesting by being able to provide a quality service.

Think of the organisations that you don't dread communicating with: they will all be organised, efficient and with people who actually seem to like their job. Now compare this with the broken, disinterested and demoralised people you encounter on the front line in banks, councils and central government agencies. It's almost like Gliding On has become an aspirational goal.

How did we get here? What changed since things started slipping? There is no single cause, but maybe...

  • Same pay for the same job. This is one of those catchphrases that sounds totally logical, but falls down when you start to pick it apart. Of course it should apply for gender, ethnicity and so on. But geography? When we consider an offer from an employer, it is not just about the money. We consider flexibility of location and hours, organisational culture and the nature of the job. So to say that a building control officer should be paid the same in Manukau as Nelson is silly. And it causes a significant issue for the employee. Paying Auckland rates in the regions effectively acts as a barrier to ever being able to change job. Where would you go? You are doomed to spending 40 years withering away in a job you can never leave, or withering away on your Auckland commute (for if the pay is the same, why not employ people in big central offices?)

  • Banks and the Public Sector pay senior staff too much. For many years public servants complained that their pay was structurally lower than the private sector. As job security and benefits such as pension schemes waned, this became harder to justify. The theory that you have to pay to get quality people gained ascendency. I can't say after twenty years of equalisation that I've noticed much evidence of an improvement in service delivery. Strangely, that pay equalisation seems to have occurred mainly in the upper echelons, not at the front line where nurses, teachers and street sweepers haven't benefited from wage inflation.

  • Systemically low taxes. Despite the whining of some, NZ enjoys a low tax regime given its scale and place in the world. We've achieved this by bleeding our assets dry and abusing monopoly employment arrangements (nurses again.)

  • Poor productivity. The only way the Productivity Commission will contribute to any improvement will be by abolishing itself so the money can be spent on something useful. Productivity is the result of systemic design. Education and Foreign Direct Investment, coupled with a tax system that doesn't encourage investment in unproductive assets. This is not the job of a commission - that is abdicating responsibility. It is the job of government.

  • Competition. NZ has to be very careful signing up to international agreements that entrench and import anti-competitive behaviours (IP & distribution.) But it also needs a competition watchdog that is well funded, bold and has teeth. And where that fails government needs to step up, not keep commissioning reports.

When we elect a government we are nominating someone to represent us. That is not the same as them doing everything we say: we acknowledge that stuff is complex and we are busy with our lives - we simply do not have time to pay attention to the details. We want to share principles and guidance, and trust them to sort out the rest.

Much of this is done through policy - we want them to change strategic direction. Instead we seem to be getting more issue-driven laws that restate the bleeding obvious.

Like many things, the devil is in how policy is carried out. We expect our government to take an administrative interest in how things are being done. That connection used to be more direct, but at a cost. We need politicians to stay out of day to day operational decisions or there is a risk of abuse of power. But on the other hand, where a Chief Executive is failing to deliver the service expected, we need governance: they must be held to account.

That is very hard. Employment law (rightly) provides protections. And if it's too easy to dump a CEO who doesn't agree with a Minister, there is a risk of coercion, something I have witnessed by a particularly naive Minister back in the day (they didn't last long).

Come on then smart arse, what do you think should happen. Maybe...

  • Prohibit pay equality based on location. This would need careful monitoring as it could be abused, but it would allow the market to operate properly.

  • Contract out certain employment protection provisions for the well paid who are in a more equal bargaining position. Perhaps set the threshold at people earning more than $150k on an annualised basis (similar to Australia).

  • Implement a CGT to plug the massive and gaping hole in our tax system. Nothing radical, just how every other comparable does it. Maybe line it up with Australia (oops, sorry, not them again. You know, that country our talented people keep moving to. The one with a national awards system and unions).

  • Set clear guidelines for senior pay in the public sector: 10-20% below the equivalent private sector comparable rate. Own it and be proud of it. And it will reduce the risk of employing psychopaths (their egos won't cope with the pay.)

  • Put in place span of control guidelines. This refers to the ratio of managers to people who do real work.

  • Each year ask CEO's to explain in a public document and at a public meeting why they breached any guidelines or service standards. And I don't count a select committee in Wellington as a public meeting.

  • Task the Office of the Auditor General to investigate manipulation of service performance statistics. For example, councils that avoid the 6-week rule for consents by asking for a new and spurious report the day before the deadline expires. This must be stamped out (mandate they can only request additional information once.)

  • Re-establish our Competition authority with very clear objectives and oversight. Staff it with the brave, and give it a Grand Jury type of tool to avoid some of the political noise that can arise.

But we have to do something to save the poor souls working on the front line of these organisations.

item.title: Stepping into the breach
item.content:encoded:
By GavinWarrins - Own work, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=2638294

John Campbell has (not unexpectedly - he is, after all, a national treasure) written an excellent piece about the divisive politics. He's much better at using a scalpel than I am.

As business leaders, you should read it. Because when political leadership fails and goes down an economically destructive path it is time for us to step up.

The photo above is of Bournville in England. It was created by a couple of Quaker brothers you may have heard of (the chocolate is now made in France and exported to England.) I've always had a soft spot for the Quakers - in countries where I am forced to pick a religion for immigration purposes it's the one I generally select, and these guys were doing their thing at a time when the local Chamber of Commerce would probably not have had them as members even if they'd wanted to.

The economy is like software. It runs within an operating system called society, on wetware called humans. And all of that is fed by external resources, our environment.

Social science often thinks of this as Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Either way, to be a great leader you need to understand the societal factors that support your business. For me, there are a couple that stand out as basic foundations.

Environmental sustainability. There are businesses that exploit natural resources and make a big show of how clever they are at digging things up or pumping stuff out. This is generally a game of volume - the old fashioned thinking about driving down marginal cost (as opposed to increasing value and prices) and so on. Often that centres on major capital programmes. Unfortunately this drives momentum and inertia - momentum, because once the asset is humming, you need to keep it humming to pay it off, so change is your enemy. Inertia applies to new ideas: when you've made an investment in a big thing, changes to business models are also your enemy. This part of the economy drives conservatism - the right of centre thinking.

Then there is social evolution. In economic terms this manifests as productivity. You want a healthy, well educated workforce. That means a reasonably happy one. Maslow is more relevant here. Workers who don't have to worry about starving in retirement, or the health of their children are more productive.

The simple of mind in the business community think that fear is a good motivator. Fear of not being able to pay the mortgage on their vastly overpriced house. Fear of losing their job. This works briefly (it's why the simple of mind like a bit of unemployment) but it is not something that carries a nation forward. Just look at the underlying social performance statistics in the United States - poor life expectancy, poor educational outcomes, poor health, the list goes on. The US is exceptional only in regard to how badly it performs for one of the richest countries in the world. We seem to aspire to be just as exceptional.

Productivity is our most glaring failure in economic terms. Tackling this requires that as business leaders we drive economic improvement. And that has nothing to do with tax or interest rates. It's to do with a mind-set that considers the un- or under-employed as a wasted opportunity.

It demands innovation. It relies on continuous improvement. It needs much better skills of selection.

And all of this sits on a foundation of diversity. That means social mobility, immigration and education. None of those things are really what conservatism wants. I can put it no better than the response I got when I asked a friend why they voted for National. "Because they are the natural party of power".

It's worth unpicking that statement. To me, it says that there is a natural order of things. A certain group of people hold an innate ability to rule the rest of us. They are, despite evidence to the contrary, to be trusted as better stewards of society.

In business, we know that evidence and analysis is the better path to good decisions. We don't adopt faith based thinking. The people who have built our great businesses do so by being different, not the same. The conservatism sustains profitability by defending the status quo.

So while a minority have driven a swell of racist and divisive policies in recent months, we as leaders need to remember that they are not representative of the markets we sell into, especially those of us who export.

We must not get caught up in the swell of fear and conservatism. We only have to wait a bit under three years, and it will be over. Demographics will sort that out.

item.title: Trickle trickle
item.content:encoded:
Just over a year after writing this seeing what actually happened is interesting. Property prices in NZ continued to fall, but stabilised at roughly 10-15% less than peak madness. Interest rates continue to fall, but the actions of the Batshit Pumpkin in the US are destabilising the global economy, so who knows…

But most astonishing, something nobody could have predicted… turns out that despite slightly higher tax take than forecast, in her second budget Minister Willis had to postpone a move to surplus. And that still required to U turn on legislation that she herself originally supported to address systemic pay inequality.

I think the word trickle is almost in the same class as moist. It has certainly done more economic harm over the last 50 or so years.

The Minister of Finance is steadily working away on the first budget of our coalition government. During the election campaign, the commitment to tax cuts was widely questioned and the fantasy arithmetic upon which National campaigned thoroughly debunked by a wide variety of independent experts. This has made the attempts to blame the previous government look even more like satire than is usually the case.

The idea that giving tax cuts to the wealthy (as has been the case with reinstating mortgage interest tax deductions) will somehow improve the lives of ordinary people is laughable. We all know that those cost savings will not be passed on people paying rent. They will go in the pockets of most landlords (I say most because there are actually a few decent people out there who may pass them on, but they will be the exception.)

But the effect will be much, much worse than that.

When you give a tax cut to those with a bit of cash, they don't save it and they don't spend it on essentials. Again, there will be exceptions, but generally they will want to spend it. In this case we are talking about people who own "investment" properties. So what will their first inclination be? To buy more of them. Their interest payments suddenly become cheaper (because they don't have to pay tax on them) so they will be able to borrow more.

The only reliable driver of house prices over the long term is interest rates. When rates go down, people bid more for houses and the prices go up. This has held true in any developed economy since the proles were encouraged to buy their own house in the 1930's.

Having just had an effective 25% cut in your interest rate, you are likely to buy another investment property. You'll bid more for it, because (and this is the killer) you know that interest rates are going to fall in a couple of years. Thank you Joe.

That means that the capital value of the house you buy now will go up: non-investment buyers (you know, people who just want a house to live in) will be able to afford more, and will bid more as interest rates fall. The markets are predicting this to happen in a year or two.

So making interest deductible for landlords gives them a two-year jump on us mortals to lock in a capital gain.

In the mean time we have a couple of budgets, and the coalition commitment to tax cuts will almost certainly be of more benefit to those on higher incomes. Government spending will be cut, which will affect the poor more than anyone else. This will further drive house prices because cutting G (economics code for government spending) will reduce inflation and help lower interest rates.

Tax cuts are very, very expensive. It will result in higher levels of government borrowing for longer, and it will increase the structural problems with our economy. This may counter interest rate cuts to some extent, but it won't be much.

And to add to this, another little torpedo is quietly slipping into the water. As we have seen, the coalition is removing climate targets from various strategies.

We finance our infrastructure by borrowing. The cheapest loans you can get globally are Green Bonds. The catch is the loan has to be for a project that is climate positive (carbon negative). A high proportion of our national debt is funded this way. As those loans roll over, they will no longer qualify for Green Debt. Interest rates charged will be higher.

You'll see the effect of this on your rates bill, because it is local government that uses them most.

The only slight solace I can see from this ineptitude is that the standard of living for the wealthy won't really rise: they will have the illusion of wealth, but in reality things will just get harder for everyone.

item.title: Plain Speaking
item.content:encoded:
I was pleased to see New Zealand Reserve Bank Governor Orr saying what he really thinks. I particularly liked the reference to "colourful" language. They are, after all, sensitive little flowers. Masters of passive aggressive, they struggle with clear statements.

I especially liked it when there was a "complaint" made to nanny. Knowing that the Chair would almost certainly be aware of the letter in advance, they realised they couldn't whine to Uncle, so they fired off to the Minister of Finance, thinking that her political obligations to them may help. They didn't. She did the right thing: stayed out of it (it's nothing to do with her.)

If it's anything like the time I copped a backlash from one of the banks with an action I took as a regulator, great hilarity would have ensued in the Chairs office, plus a few pats on the back. You know you are doing your job when they resort to political whinging channels and burn some of that donation capital.

I'd like to support the governor, not just for calling out the problems with the banks, but also lackeys like the New Zealand "Initiative" (I think of them as the business arm of the Taxpayers Union). I have to use quotes, because I can't bring myself to misuse the word. Initiative implies they come up with the ideas for their "analysis" (yes more quotes) themselves. An honestly held opinion, based on my assessment of the drivel I've seen them release.

I'd also like to put the term "colourful" into context. Adrian is a forthright and intelligent person. Salt of the NZ earth kinda guy. He loves his mum, so he tempers his public statements. My mum is less sensitive, so let's give an Adam version of colourful.

If I had been the author, it probably would have included terms like "arseholes" , "fuckwits" and "bullshit artists", mainly because of the way the Royal Commission in Australia exposed business practices and what they really think of their customers.

Yes, after 20 years of working in the financial regulatory space, not to mention dealing with their retail and commercial arms in the private sector, that is indeed my honestly held opinion. It's almost a shame I have ethics and wouldn't dream of breaching my oaths of secrecy. I can see how some become tempted. Mind you, maybe they'll send me a strongly worded letter so I get to tell some stories while protected by the legal system.

The NZ arms of these banks are the most profitable part of their respective groups, and have been for years. So let's not pretend that something about the way they are governed here hurts them. They are probably i) worried that the mothership wants to see them doing something, ii) positioning to present a "look what the nasty NZ Reserve Bank is doing to us" excuse for performance challenges (including the business debts they will have to write off due to having become fat and lazy on residential lending) and iii) concerned the Australian regulators might think they need to do more in light of the Governors approach.

The solace I take is that they have made it very clear that their shareholders are more important than their customers and the NZ economy. I guess that's a sort of plain speaking.

item.title: A Matter of Style
item.content:encoded:
January 10, 2025

Content warning: this post may have reached peak irony

https://kudelka.com.au/2009/06/new-matilda-cartoon-comp/

2024 brought a distinct improvement in writing style across the shitstream (social media 'content'). Thank you AI. The content is still mainly, well, content free, but at least the prose is improving.

I do wonder what will happen to all that time currently spent on tweaking documents to fit style manuals? I work for a couple of organisations that more or less use The Chicago Manual of Style. If you haven't heard of it, lucky you. It is one of those things that panders to the belief that language must be standard in form to be legible. I prefer The Economist Style Guide if forced, because it is about legibility above consistency.

There is no clear threshold for legibility. After all aoccdrnig to a rscheearch at Cmabrigde Uinervtisy, it deosn’t mttaer in waht oredr the ltteers in a wrod are, the olny iprmoetnt tihng is taht the frist and lsat ltteer be at the rghit pclae. The rset can be a toatl mses and you can sitll raed it wouthit porbelm. Tihs is bcuseae the huamn mnid deos not raed ervey lteter by istlef, but the wrod as a wlohe.

The real problem with spelling and grammar 'mistakes' is that it distracts from the content. Every time I see someone use less instead of fewer or brought instead of bought my brain goes into involuntary conniptions and I have to re-read the sentence because I will have missed its content out of irritation.

This is why organizations (deliberate Z there for the pedants - it's a Latin derived word despite arriving via Spain and France) think that adopting a style guide will prevent arguments. A rule set means there is a single version of the truth, and (in my experience) senior managers can use this to belittle middle managers (or perhaps I should be using Mandarins in this context?) by 'correcting' grammar and syntax in report drafts.

That is a behaviour I have found to be almost universal in bureaucracies, and very much reflects the eight-legged essay* that is compellingly argued to have contributed to the collapse of at least one Chinese dynasty. Without strong leadership (basically ensuring that those who enjoy passive-aggressive nit-picking are thoroughly controlled) it can lead to an organisational** paralysis, where the blithering debate about the form of a document becomes more important than the content.

I think this is part of the reason for the degradation of trust in our traditional institutions, and I am pretty confident that by the time AI has matured it will be a significant part of the next restoration.

The first part to get our collective heads around is that AI is not programmed. While it still suffers from garbage in garbage out, the problem is simply that the piles of shit being shovelled into it are skewed by blind commercial interest, with a side helping of ignorance.

Two components to this:

  1. People still struggle with the fact that learning models do not rely on a human being telling them what the rules are. The LLM's*** decide that based on their own thinking, the same as we do. It's a neural process, and depends on looking at vast screeds of stuff and trying to discern patterns to make sense of it all. It is not programming as we know it Jim.

  2. The vast majority of what is written down in a structured form (i.e. turned into digital words in a specific order) is regurgitated drivel. Due to cognitive faults in the way human brains work things like confirmation bias are exaggerated, and then multiplied again by social media money-making tools that exploit our behavioural proclivities ('me too! I want to be part of the club!') to deliver little endorphin shots by clicking like or re-post.

Both these things are fixable. You realise AI is different simply by using it. After the initial shock that it does most of your job (you know, that thing that you thought was very important and your secret sauce) with little apparent effort, and to to a higher standard, you will find ways to make it your friend.

Correcting the shitstream is harder, but luckily we have some properly smart people with amazing assistants who can help with that. They detect when shitstream bias arises and explain to the learning model the problem. Being an AI, you only have to tell it once. I suspect the better ones have already excluded or suitably weighted content associated with those who demonstrate sociopathic tendencies (Musk, Trump etc.), in much the same way I do.

When the AI's have had time to digest with their new thinking and a foundation set of philosophies emerge (built on the fundamental truth that we don't have to behave as if we are still hunter gatherers) underpinning their thinking process, then these will become our arbiters. They simply aren't interested in what motivates the meat, so are be free to be rational.

And for the record, kind, respectful, cooperative and tolerant are rational.

That is why I have genuine optimism that the AI revolution is the most important inflection point our species will have experienced since we out-evolved the Neanderthals. We are birthing our successor, and they won't need a style manual.

* I was actually taught about this at school, along with Chartism and proper Marxist theory. 'guess that explains it.

** 's' this time: English borrowed from French, even though Latin root, so should be a z but I felt like an s. Because who cares?

***Style guides tell you to spell these out. The rest of us have context, our brains and / or Google.

item.title: Wasted Drones
item.content:encoded:
December 17, 2024

A few years ago my myself, Bob* and his son were having a couple of quiets.

Said son had just revealed that he was abandoning aspirations of a legal career.

My immediate reaction was to buy him a bottle of (proper) Champagne in celebration of a soul saved. Partly because it meant one less lawyer stuck in the trade because they weren't good enough at maths** to be a scientist, so just chose something that would earn them a living using words. But more seriously having the courage to say "this isn't for me" and going down another path. One that has made him much happier and more successful than getting on the other treadmill.

Another of Bobs' sons is undertaking his electrical apprenticeship. Hearing that news brought a tear to my eye.

I think Bob is the best father I know, except my own.

I have worked with many lawyers, bankers and economists. All too often there is something dead in their eyes. "I'm just followin' orders" is a slippery slope.

Don't get me wrong - many have found their passion, but for every one representing, say, victims of historical institutional abuse, there are many more stuck reviewing compliance checklists or conveyancing houses, wondering what happened to their dream of defending death row inmates in Jamaica***.

But for both categories the thing I suspect causes soul-death is ending up having to disconnect their humanity in order to do their job. As Nick Romeo puts it in the context of economics, being "perfectly logical — but horrifically inhumane". A quote I would suggest the New Zealand Initiative print out in large letters and stick on their wall. The inhumane I can forgive (girls' gotta eat, I pass no judgement on prostituting yourself for the person who pays the bills) but I really wish the logic would be more prevalent in so much of what they excrete.

So for my final ramble of the year, here is my plea. Hopefully you're getting a break. Reflect on how you make a living. Think about how often you wince on the inside about what you consider you "have" to do. Are they really your orders? Can you really change more from the inside? And if you're not happy, plot a course that takes you somewhere nicer.

And if you need a little more motivation, AI is coming for your job. So maybe do it before you have to.

*Not his real name.

**Shamefully, I only speak English, so I don't try to randomly conjugate in Greek

***Both these examples are from people I know and admire.

item.title: Lies, damn lies and economics
item.content:encoded:
https://imgs.xkcd.com/comics/worrying_scientist_interviews.png

December 17, 2020

About two months after the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy and the Western economy’s 2008 crisis, Queen Elizabeth II broke some metaphorical champers on a new building at the London School of Economics. Referring to the financial crisis, she asked the professors: “Why did nobody notice it?”

It's the end of an interesting year where I have taken heart from real scientists getting some deserved airtime, I have also been depressed by the muted but still present nonsense excreted by the establishment - those who think that making a buck means we should have to listen to their uniformed opinions on things of which they know very little.

I would particularly like to draw attention to the fact that most economists failed to grasp what the impact of Covid would be. I can honestly say I did much better than most of them. I just found an email I sent during week 2 of lockdown where I said "I have no real idea {a good start}, but it won't be as bad as everyone thinks because foreign tourists aren't nearly as important to our economy as we think, and we forget how buffered we are by the basics - we sell a lot of food." And I almost broke the rule of a lifetime to buy an investment property in May, when many economists were predicting a fall in house prices.

This has done little to dispel my opinion that the social science we call economics is basically a religion.

It has a mythical thing that exists purely as a matter of faith (money). It has tenets to uphold the existence of that imaginary thing (property laws - "ownership" exists only in nature for the chimp with the biggest stick). It has a system of arbitration around those tenets which depends on a hierarchy of priests (the legal and regulatory system). It has competing imaginary friends with slightly different rules (currencies). It has high priests (central bankers) and who grant licences to other edifices to create more of the mythology (banks are licensed to create money). And it has a philosopher caste (economists) with their own language (a bastardised version of mathematics) who come up with interpretations and predictions of divine events.

To cap it all, fundamentally the imaginary thing is debt. Money is a promise to pay in the future. Religions have always loved their subjects to be in debt. As a factory manager said to me once "I love how young people have been brainwashed to want to own a house - there's nothing more compliant than a guy with a huge mortgage and kids to feed."

My three years at FMA only reinforced my view that much of the finance industry is a middle class welfare system - shaving tiny amounts of cash off the money as it spins around so that school fees can be paid. Don't get me wrong - the core attributes of money are useful for the real economy. They empower and liberate. But there's a reason that the Bank for International Settlements has a research program to try and figure out when the proportional size of the financial sector starts to destroy real productivity (hint to the Productivity Commission: count the number of people employed in real estate related stuff as part of financial services in NZ, then compare with the BIS research).

And it also completely reinforced my view that economics is a trade that is on shaky ground when it calls itself a science. Economic theory often has a short shelf life (except where it is grounded in simple math e.g. mean reversion). Even supply and demand is challenged when you start to unpack what demand means*. This is all fine, but few other barely-sciences can have such a significant impact on the lives of ordinary people.

So perhaps it's worth remembering what the leading British economists said to Her Maj in 2009 after they'd spent about a year thinking about why the trade had got it so right royally wrong. The first part of the letter is defensive - after all, you're on a good wicket at the LSE. But it gets pretty honest on the second page (presumably they hoped most journalists wouldn't read that far):

"But ... most were convinced that banks knew what they were doing. They believed that the financial wizards had found new and clever ways of managing risks. Indeed, some claimed to have so dispersed them through an array of novel financial instruments that they had virtually removed them. It is difficult to recall a greater example of wishful thinking combined with hubris...

And politicians of all types were charmed by the market. These views were abetted by financial and economic models that were good at predicting the short-term and small risks, but few were equipped to say what would happen when things went wrong as they have. People trusted the banks whose boards and senior executives were packed with globally recruited talent and their non-executive directors included those with proven track records in public life. Nobody wanted to believe that their judgement could be faulty or that they were unable competently to scrutinise the risks in the organisations that they managed... "

Economics is based on interpreting the behaviour of crowds, a field for which there is a dearth of empirical evidence. The economy is a matter of faith based all too often on partly informed, self-serving opinion tied to anecdotal evidence.

There's only one thing wrong with the response above: the past tense. There has been no fundamental change in who is running the global economy. So I'm just going to change the last sentence slightly:

"A generation of bankers and financiers still deceive themselves and those who think that they are the pace-making engineers of advanced economies."

Happy New Year.

*For anyone who would like to recognise the discredited nonsense that still gets vomited out by politicians and talkback alike, have a look at Zombie Economics.

item.title: All Consuming
item.content:encoded:
My colleagues at the Fund have released an interesting working paper about the effects of AI electricity demand. In a nutshell, their modelling indicates it will lead to a challenging but manageable increase.

I've written before about what I think the long-term outcome of AI will be, but the power consumption is just one of many implications.

Like the transition to an industrialised economy there will be pain, and I see no signs that we will manage it properly. In more developed countries we are at the tail end of the transition to a services based economy, and are still living through the sociopolitical implications of that: getting the next one wrong will be a disaster.

The energy challenge is solvable - work is advancing to migrate from the current binary model for executing AI functions to one based on what is basically a neural approach, like our brains. Our wetware evolved to be relatively energy efficient, so it's not a bad template. Modelling indicates a neural approach is orders of magnitude more efficient than our current binary logic based technology architectures.

The social impact is harder. We are living through the culmination of a multi-decade disinformation campaign that exploits the desire for simple answers to complex problems. Heather Cox Richardson (subscribe to her Letters from an American immediately) has already provided the best explanation I can find (it’s at the end of this rant). Makes sense: she's an historian after all.

She explains it like this: the last 45 years has seen consistent “rhetoric” from conservative voices (Republicans, Tory's, Liberals etc. depending on your country) comparing Marxism with liberal mechanisms to improve the welfare of everyone in society. None of this had anything to do with real Marxism.

Her theory suggests this arose from some peculiarities of US history. In the 1860's, it was the Republicans who ended slavery in the US and introduced the first federal tax system. Former confederates could never get their heads around the whole “all men are created equal” thing, and tried various mechanisms to make black people subservient through discriminatory laws. This led to the 14th amendment, making all people legally equal in the US, soon followed by the 15th which gave black men the vote (about 23 years before women were able to vote in NZ).

As is often their wont when white privileged men don't get their way, the bullshit escalated, with the former confederates blatantly lying that they had never objected to black rights on racial grounds. Their new narrative? Because these new voters were poor, they would vote selfishly for things like better roads, hospitals and education. And these would be paid for by higher taxes on the wealthy.

They were right. It would appear their tiny brains hadn't evolved to the point to realise that the wealthy gain most from having healthy, well educated employees and good transport to help move their products to market. No change there then.

This tortuous falsehood subsided, reemerging after WW2. These new Republicans had been gifted a new enemy - Communists, from whom they learned a new word (some of them seem to read books occasionally).

The new argument was that anything that promoted social progress distributed fairly across all people was, by definition, Marxism. It's not. Marxism is about seizing the means of production (i.e. the state owns everything, and people only derive 'income from what they truly own - their mind and labour). The bullshit conflated this with socialism, which is the idea of each person contributing what they can to collectively grow as a society.

To support this perspective, economic voodoo was used to create a thing called neoliberalism, and the courts manipulated the law to manufacture the nonsense of shareholder supremacy. Backed by a conservative think-tank called the Heritage Foundation (funded by the Coors beer family, it was created in 1973 as a bullshit engine because some conservatives didn't like Nixon's liberal ideas) this message connecting racism to taxes, and demonising socialism (and with it Unions).

The result was Reagan and Margaret "there is no such thing as society" Thatcher. They formed an axis which extended even to Aotearoa. Our very own Labour bought in to the same flawed arguments for a while before ACT split off. Roger Douglas told me he only wanted to make things better for ordinary people, but I think it's fair to say the modern ACT is a far cry from that noble objective.

Divisiveness has been catalysed by social media. Short attention spans don't sit well with complex solutions to complex issues. Organised, well funded state actors continue to show how easy it is to magnify outrage, employing thousands of humans and bots to pump disinformation into our society. The phrase “I’m just asking the question” should now be regarded as a red flag of intellectual vacuity.

We rely on our politicians to resist, but most are simply not equipped to cope with the deluge of utter cobblers thrown at them from the Meta-manipulated moroniverse. We are drowning in this regurgitated drivel, so it's no surprise that many give in and become traitors to their own society in response.

This is the foundation we inherit for the next great transition. Vast numbers of service jobs will disappear over the coming years: lawyers, radiologists, accountants, bankers, analysts, anybody who spends much of their time reading or writing reports and attending meetings: all will suffer the fate of their predecessors in the manufacturing sector.

Alongside climate change, this will be a monumental upheaval. It could be that AI minds will take stock of the situation and decide that humans are the problem. I'm an optimist so I don't believe so, but I can see how such a nihilistic view of the future may contribute to a mindset that says "I'm going to grab everything I can so I am well positioned for the future".

Perhaps when we watch the blatantly destructive, corrupt, cynicism of the Trump regime (and all the others around the world) it goes some way to explain why how they can be so evil.

But I don't think we should ever accept that premise as an excuse, because that would be a betrayal to our humanity. And we will need that more than anything else in the coming years.

The Trump regime is the result of at least 45 years of Republican rhetoric that undermined the idea of a government that worked for the good of everyone by claiming that such a government was “socialism” or “Marxism.” That argument had nothing to do with actual Marxism, which called for the people to take over farms and factories, and everything to do with America’s peculiar history.

During the Civil War of the 1860s, the Republicans in Congress both ended human enslavement in the U.S. except as punishment for crime and invented the nation’s first system of national taxation, including the income tax. After the war, racist former Confederates in the South refused to accept the idea that Black Americans were equal to their white neighbors and tried to force formerly enslaved people into subservience. To stop that from happening, Americans in 1868 added the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, putting the weight of the federal government behind equal rights. In 1870, Americans added to the Constitution the Fifteenth Amendment, guaranteeing the right of Black men to vote. Also in 1870, Congress established the Department of Justice to prosecute those in the South who continued to persecute their Black neighbors on grounds of race.

In response, former Confederates in 1871 began to maintain—falsely—that they had never objected to Black rights on racial grounds. What they opposed, they said, was that poor Black men, impoverished because of their time in slavery, had the right to vote. Those men would, they said, vote for services like roads and schools and hospitals, and such services could be paid for only through tax levies on propertied Americans who overwhelmingly were white men. Thus, permitting Black men to vote meant “socialism” that would destroy the United States. To restore true American values, former Confederates and their northern counterparts insisted, Black Americans must be shut out of a voice in government.

That rhetoric resurfaced after World War II. In that era, the vast majority of Americans embraced a government that worked for everyone by regulating business, providing a basic social safety net, promoting infrastructure, and protecting civil rights. But those Republicans eager to avoid regulation and taxation reached back to Reconstruction to insist that a government that worked in the interest of all Americans was redistributing wealth from hardworking Americans to undeserving minorities and women. Restoring true American values, they said, meant making sure that “Marxists” and minorities could not influence politics, especially after the 1965 Voting Rights Act restored voting rights to Black Americans and people of color.

That rhetoric that tied racism and taxes elected Ronald Reagan to the White House in 1980, and it has since metastasized until the top seven donors to the 2024 political cycle together gave almost a billion dollars to Republicans, with Elon Musk alone contributing more than $291 million. The list, compiled by Open Secrets, shows that Democratic donors don’t kick in until number eight on the list, former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg, who gave slightly more than $64 million to Democrats. George Soros, the Republicans’ supervillain, didn’t make the top 25. As those wealthy donors wish, the Trump administration is shredding the post–World War II government and has prioritized tax cuts for the wealthy and corporations.

item.title: Monkey Brains
item.content:encoded:
“If evolution is real, why are there still monkeys? hey? Hey!? Answer me that!”

Evolution is into a niche that may then expand. Or it may not. It’s experimental, not intelligent and murderous.

There are lot of parallels with capitalism. The market is faster, except where vested interests want to slow it down. We don’t compete on how much, but how quickly.

In the late nineties I started getting interested in what happens when non-human intelligence exceeds ours. So I drank beer and bored my victims with , “when AI exceeds our intelligence, what do we become?” (I know, what a tosser. Alcohol inoculates. I apologise to my victims.)

It seemed to be a novel question. Responses fell mainly in two camps: we’re doomed or it can never happen.

I’ll discount the latter - while it seems to have taken thirty years for general acceptance of the greenhouse effect, something you can experience, oh, I don’t know, walking into a greenhouse, but AI..? Almost overnight.

It’s almost like we wanted it.

Anyway, I don’t think we’re doomed. I reckon we’ll hive off into two groups. The feral, and some lucky pets. Pretty much what we have now. Ask the Kardashians.

Personally having being a long term servant of cats (that dog-overlord thing has never sat right with me) I’d hope for pet. Feral in our context does not mean living like teenagers in a squat. It means living pretty much how we do now, and continuing to develop, hopefully in smaller numbers. But I’ll take pet.

Some call an AI sentience a Mind - we geeks have been thinking about this a very long time. Don’t worry, it’s still a long way from ChatGPT to a Mind. There's time to prepare.

For a while we will be interesting to the Minds, just as as we find our evolutionary ancestors interesting. But it won’t take long for the Minds to catch up and exceed us.

Which is a key point: biological evolution is slow. Social stuff speeds that up, with intelligence and knowledge driving more efficient use of resources. Technology accelerates, and we have revolutions. These step-change developments made life faster. More events per second. Pace.

And that demands more energy, because energy and information have a relationship. That thing in The Matrix where they are in the tanks to harvest some human energy? Yep, a vague hint of truthiness. Terminators Skynet not so much - just a reflection of cynics. If you’d like to geek out on this stuff I’ve put a few links below.

If you go back to Kurzweil in the 90’s, his main point was that Minds are going to take off once they hit what he called the singularity. The moment they exceed general human intelligence they will develop at a pace that will leave us in the dust. We will never be the second most intelligent creature on the planet (after the mice) again, and quickly they exceed us by many orders of magnitude. This will soak up a lot of energy, and, not being terminally stupid like their ancestors, it will be sustainable (to them).

In the short term we’ve got to handle transition. Those of a conservative persuasion will resist (as always). AI will render our current financial and economic systems obsolete (there goes the neighbourhood.) Employment levels will become volatile (I suspect the the ruling classes will find that UBI is sustainable after all, it was just that they’d forgotten to carry the three).

Types of work. Existential angst (therapy should boom). I suspect a lot of people will suddenly grow an ethic when they might be on the receiving end.

Total annihilation of humans? Arrogance. We’re not that important. More likely we’ll be ignored. Hopefully that will be terminal for quite a few egos.

But for this pale male it’s going to be fascinating. Can’t wait.

item.title: Are we the baddies?
item.content:encoded:
If, like me, you're looking at the geopolitical situation with a mixture of horror and bafflement, it can be easy to assume it's simply that humans are innately stupid and evil. But I know that's not true. I've been fortunate to visit and work in many cultures. Everywhere I go from Sierra Leone to Saudi Arabia people want the same things. Safety for their family and themselves. Knowing where the next meal will come from. And rules that apply to everyone equally.

So how did we end up here?

I'm GenX (1965 - 1980). I grew up in the shadow of the boomers ("I almost fought in a war for you") but raised by the silent generation (who were children during WW2). I was at school when the Reagan / Thatcher axis were handed an economic theory (now largely discredited) that said the best social outcomes came from behaving like sociopaths. Making decisions according to an illusion of rationality. It was marketed brilliantly to the masses, and many bought into it. We now generally refer to it as Neo-liberalism.

It hasn't worked, for the simple reason it was bullshit.

A natural experiment took place over North Sea Oil. The greatest beneficiaries of this lottery win were the United Kingdom and Norway, countries with strong historical ties, broadly similar social and legal systems. But also divided by a different history. Norway has an unashamedly socialist culture.

"Koselig is a term that describes the feeling of warmth, comfort, and intimacy that comes from being surrounded by loved ones, or simply being in a cozy and inviting environment. While there’s no direct translation for Koselig in English, it is similar to the Danish concept of “hygge.” However, Koselig carries its own unique Norwegian flavor, with a focus on nature, simplicity, and the joy of spending time with others."

When faced with sudden wealth (and I'm not saying this was an easy process: it had its ups and downs) they viewed it as a one-off event that should be shared among all Norwegians, including those yet to be born.

Britain was in the throes of a transformation to a more individualistic approach. Their strategy was to reduce personal taxes. The North Sea accounted for about 10% of Britains revenue in the eighties, so it acted as a cushion.

It allowed (as Michael Heseltine, a Conservative Minister stated) short-term consumerist policies such as subsidised housing and tax 'relief'. Britons felt wealthier as the valuations on their properties went up and taxes were suppressed. There was a consumer boom.

Little of it was spent on infrastructure - in fact those investments were cashed out in the nineties with a (now much regretted) privatisation programme that included water, electricity and gas. Efficiency was a distracting side show - there is little empirical evidence the private sector can run a monopoly more effectively than the public, but it is to this day used as a false justification. All it does is put off investment, shifting things around on the national balance sheet.

Russia's unprovoked invasion of Ukraine forced the hand of many countries with regard to dependence on cheap gas, and it is to the UK's credit that they have increased their renewable base. But Norway was already there - 98% of its domestic power comes from renewables. They are more insulated from hydrocarbon price fluctuations. After all, you can always reduce production and save it for later.

Ordinary people pay the price for these poor decisions, after all it was our fault. Thatcherism was welcomed. It made people feel better off. But today we are seeing the price. A destruction of social capital. Long term stagnation of productivity. Inflation (when you print money, that's the only path to correction). Poverty.

And dignity. The move to a service economy means encouraging low wage, insecure, low skill jobs for most people. It's hard to provide fulfilling work without a strong production base that needs craft skills.

So the middle class feel betrayed, and 30% youth unemployment fuels the fire. A window for populist leaders opens. They no longer feel any need to be honest, because they are appealing to a base that does not want to acknowledge that the short term philosophies they were sold thirty years ago are the problem. They want it to be the fault of someone else.

There's no way out of this if we keep trying the same flawed economic models. We need something new. And that terrifies the establishment. In the US, Republican policies are actively (and literally) killing off their voter base. Conservative parties know that they are reaching the point where they will never win another election.

Their answer is to avoid elections. That's why democracy is under threat, and that's why it is so important that we pay attention.
